Qatāda said: By Allah, no people forgot the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except that they were ruined and corrupted.

The meaning: "We did not lead them astray, but they went astray."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

That is, the worshipped denied you by your saying about them that they are gods and partners, or by your saying that they commanded you to worship them and called you to it.

It was said: the address is to the believers in this world: that is, these polytheists have denied you, O believers, in what you say, which Muḥammad (ﷺ) brought from Allah of monotheism and faith. The first is more apparent, and the context indicates it.

As for one who reads it with the letter of the third person (yaqūlūna), the meaning is: "they have denied you by their statement," then He said:

﴿So you are not able to avert (ṣarfan) nor to obtain help (naṣran)﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

This is reporting their condition on that Day, and that they are not able to avert the punishment from themselves, nor to get help for themselves from Allah.

﴿Rather, they will today be submissive﴾ [aṣ-Ṣāffāt: 26].

This is the condition of the servants of Satan on the day of meeting the Most Merciful. Woe to their bad condition when they are separated from the believers, when they hear the call:

﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals. Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy. Al-Bawār means destruction and corruption; it is said: "bārat al-silʿa" (the merchandise became unsaleable) and "bārat al-mar'a" (the woman remained unmarried) when no one came to marry her.

Qatāda said: By Allah, no people forgot the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except that they were ruined and corrupted.

The meaning: "We did not lead them astray, but they went astray."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

That is, the worshipped denied you by your saying about them that they are gods and partners, or by your saying that they commanded you to worship them and called you to it.

It was said: the address is to the believers in this world: that is, these polytheists have denied you, O believers, in what you say, which Muḥammad (ﷺ) brought from Allah of monotheism and faith. The first is more apparent, and the context indicates it.

As for one who reads it with the letter of the third person (yaqūlūna), the meaning is: "they have denied you by their statement," then He said:

﴿So you are not able to avert (ṣarfan) nor to obtain help (naṣran)﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

This is reporting their condition on that Day, and that they are not able to avert the punishment from themselves, nor to get help for themselves from Allah.

Ibn Zayd said: On the Day of Resurrection, when the creatures are gathered, a herald will call out: whoever was worshipped besides Allah, let him not help today whoever worshipped him, and the worshipper does not help his god:

﴿Rather, they will today be submissive﴾ [aṣ-Ṣāffāt: 26].

This is the condition of the servants of Satan on the day of meeting the Most Merciful. Woe to their bad condition when they are separated from the believers, when they hear the call:

﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals. Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy. And that you worship Me; this is a straight path. And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Then did you not use reason?﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 59-62].

(Fāʾida)

He named them "His servants" despite their misguidance, but this naming was restricted by an indication (qualified). The unrestricted naming (ʿibād, without qualification) has come only for the people of the second type.

As for the second type: it is the servitude of obedience and love, and following commands. The Exalted said: ﴿O My servants, no fear shall be upon you this Day, nor shall you grieve﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 68], and He said: ﴿So give good tidings to My servants, who listen to speech and follow the best of it﴾ [az-Zumar: 17], and He said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth in humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Peace"﴾.

So all of creation are servants of His lordship (ʿubūdiyyat al-rubūbiyya), while the people of His obedience and His guardianship (wilāya) are the servants of His divinity (ʿubūdiyyat al-ilāhiyya).

The attribution of "servants" to Him in an unrestricted manner does not occur in the Qur'an except for these people.

As for describing the servants of His lordship with servitude, it comes only in one of five ways: First, indefinite (munakkaran), as in His saying: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant﴾ [Maryam: 93]. Second, definite with the article (muʿarrafan bil-lām), as in His saying: ﴿And Allah does not intend injustice to the servants﴾ [Ghāfir: 31], and ﴿Indeed, Allah has judged between the servants﴾ [Ghāfir: 48].

Third: restricted by an indication or the like, as in His saying: ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?﴾ [al-Furqān: 17].

Fourth: that they are mentioned within the general category of His servants, so they are included with the people of His obedience in the mention, as in His saying: ﴿You will judge between Your servants concerning that over which they used to differ﴾ [az-Zumar: 46].

Fifth: that they are mentioned as described by their own action, as in His saying: ﴿Say, "O My servants who have transgressed against themselves, do not despair of the mercy of Allah"﴾ [az-Zumar: 53].

It may be said: He named them His servants only because they did not despair of His mercy, turned back to Him in repentance, and followed the best of what was sent down to them from their Lord; so they become among the servants of divinity and obedience.

(Faṣl)

His saying, glorified is He: ﴿And the Day He gathers them and what they worship besides Allah﴾ [al-Furqān: 17].

This is general over every worshipper and what he worships besides Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿So He will say, "Did you lead these, My servants, astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ [al-Furqān: 17].

Mujāhid said, as narrated by Warqāʾ from Ibn Abī Najīḥ, from him: "This is an address to ʿĪsā, ʿUzayr, and the angels." Ibn Jurayj narrated similarly from him.

As for ʿIkrima, al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Kalbī, they said: it is general, covering idols and their worshippers.

Then Allah, glorified is He, permits them to speak, and He says: ﴿Did you lead these, My servants, astray?﴾ [al-Furqān: 17].

Muqātil said: He, glorified is He, says: "Did you command them to worship you, or did they themselves stray from the way?" That is, did they err from the path? The worshipped ones answered with what Allah related of their words: ﴿Glory be to You! It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ [al-Furqān: 18].

This answer is fitting only from the angels, the Messiah, and ʿUzayr, and from those whom the polytheists worshipped among the friends of Allah.

For this reason Ibn Jarīr said: Allah, His remembrance is exalted, says: the angels and ʿĪsā said, those whom these polytheists used to worship besides Allah [declaring You far above, O our Lord, and clear of what these polytheists attribute to You].

﴿It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ [al-Furqān: 18].

We would not take them as allies; rather, You are our Guardian, not them.

Ibn ʿAbbās and Muqātil said: "They exalted Allah and magnified Him, that there should be any god with Him."

There are two readings of it: the more famous is nattakhidha, with a fatḥa on the nūn and a kasra on the khāʾ, in the active voice, which is the reading of the Seven. The second is nuttakhidha, with a ḍamma on the nūn and a fatḥa on the khāʾ, in the passive voice; this is the reading of al-Ḥasan and Yazīd ibn al-Qaʿqāʿ.

Each of the two readings has a difficulty.

As for the reading of the majority, Allah, glorified is He, asked them: did they lead the polytheists astray by commanding them to worship them, or did they themselves stray from the way by their choice and desires? How can this answer correspond to the question? For He did not ask them: "Did you take besides Me any protectors?" so that they would say: ﴿It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ [al-Furqān: 18].

Rather, He asked them whether they commanded My servants to associate partners with Me, or whether they themselves associated. The corresponding answer would be for them to say: "We did not command them to associate, rather they preferred it and approved it," or "We did not command them to worship us," as He said in another verse concerning them: ﴿We disown You; they did not used to worship us﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 63].

When the proponents of the other reading saw this, they took refuge in the passive form of the verb. They said: the answer is valid and corresponds to that on this reading. The meaning becomes: "It is not fitting for us to worship and take gods; how then would we command them to do what is neither fitting nor proper for us?"

But this reading entails another difficulty, namely His saying: ﴿min awliyāʾ﴾ [al-Furqān: 18].

For the addition of "min" is good only with the intention of generality, as you say: "No man stood" (mā qāma min rajulin), and "I did not strike any man" (mā ḍarabtu min rajulin). But when the negation falls upon a specific thing, the addition of "min" is not good in it, and they only negated of themselves what was attributed to them by the claim of the polytheists, that they had commanded them to associate. So they negated of themselves that, by saying it is not becoming for them, nor fitting for them to be worshipped; how then would they call Your servants to worship them? So the necessary form according to this would be that you read: "It is not for us to take protectors besides You, or besides You protectors."

The proponents of the first reading answered with several points:

The first: the meaning is: "It was not fitting for us to worship other than You, or to take other than You as a guardian and object of worship; how then would we call anyone to worship us?" That is, since we do not worship other than You, how would we call anyone to worship us? And the meaning is that if they do not regard worship of Allah, the Exalted, as incumbent upon themselves, how could they call others to worship them? This is the answer of al-Farrāʾ.

Al-Jurjānī said: this, gradually, becomes an answer to the apparent question, which is that whoever worships something has taken it as a guardian, and when the worshipper takes it as a guardian, the worshipped becomes a guardian for the worshipper. The evidence for this is the saying of the Exalted:

﴿And the Day He gathers them all, then He says to the angels, "Did these used to worship you?" They say, "Glory be to You! You are our Guardian, not them"﴾ [Saba': 40-41].

This shows that the worshipper becomes a guardian of the worshipped.

The meaning becomes as if they had said: "It was not fitting for us to command others to take us as guardians, and to take besides You a guardian who would worship us." This is an elaboration of the statement of Ibn ʿAbbās on this verse.

He said: they say, "We did not take them as guardians, nor did we love their worship." He said: it may also be that their saying, ﴿It was not for us to take any protectors besides You﴾ [al-Furqān: 18], means that they intend the company of servants, not themselves: that is, we and they are Your servants, and it is not fitting for Your servants to take protectors besides You; but they attributed that to themselves out of humility. As a man says to one who has committed a reprehensible act: "It was not fitting for me to do such a thing," meaning: you are like me, a servant held to account; so if it is not becoming of someone like me to do this, it is not becoming of you either.

He said: Because of this difficulty, those who read nuttakhidha with a ḍamma on the nūn read it that way, and this reading is closer to the interpretation.

But al-Zajjāj said: this reading is erroneous, because you say, "I have not taken anyone as a guardian (mā ittakhadhtu min aḥadin waliyyan)," and it is not permitted to say "mā ittakhadhtu aḥadan min waliyyin," since "min" enters only because it negates one from the sense of all: you say "No one is standing (mā min aḥadin qāʾiman)," and "No man is a lover of what harms him (mā min rajulin muḥibban limā yaḍurruhu)," and it is not permitted to say "mā rajulun min muḥibbin limā yaḍurruhu."

He said: we have no justification for this at all; and if this were permitted, it would be permitted in: ﴿Then there is not of you anyone who could withhold from Him﴾ [al-Ḥāqqa: 47] — "mā aḥadun ʿanhu min ḥājizīn."

If "min" were not included, this reading would be valid.

The author of al-Naẓm said: the reason for the invalidity of this reading is that "min" enters only upon an object that has no other object before it. When there is an object preceding it other than it, "min" is not good to enter, as in His saying: ﴿It is not for Allah to take any son﴾ [Maryam: 35].

Here "min walad" has no object other than itself; if He had said, "It is not for Allah to take anyone of a son," "min" would not be good in it, because the verb of taking is occupied with "aḥad."

Others validated this reading both in wording and meaning, and made it conform to the rules of Arabic grammar.

They said: it was read by those whose eloquence is beyond doubt.

It was read by Zayd ibn Thābit, Abū al-Dardāʾ, Abū Jaʿfar, Mujāhid, Naṣr ibn ʿAlqama, Makḥūl, Zayd ibn ʿAlī, Abū Rajāʾ, al-Ḥasan, Ḥafṣ ibn Ḥumayd, and Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī, with some variation of transmission from some of them, as Abū al-Fatḥ Ibn Jinnī mentioned. He then explained it as: "min awliyāʾ" is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) phrase, meaning: it was not fitting for us to take protectors besides You. "Min" entered as a superfluous particle because of the negation, like your saying: "I took Zayd as a deputy (wakīlan)," and when you negate it you say: "I did not take Zayd as any deputy (mā ittakhadhtu Zaydan min wakīl)." Likewise: "I gave him a dirham," and "I did not give him any dirham (mā aʿṭaytuhu min dirham)." This is with regard to the object.

I say: he means that its superfluous use with the circumstantial phrase is like its superfluous use with the object.

A parallel to this is your saying: "It is not fitting for me to serve you while being lazy (mā yanbaghī lī an akhdimaka mutathāqilan)"; when you emphasize, you say: "min mutathāqil."

If it is said: both readings are valid in wording and meaning, so which is better?

I say: the reading of the majority is better and more eloquent in conveying the intended meaning and in disassociating them from what is unbecoming for them. For on the reading with a ḍamma, they would have negated that the polytheists' taking them as protectors is fitting; but on the reading of the majority, they have informed that it is not becoming for them, nor fitting for them, to take a guardian besides Him, but You alone are our Guardian and our object of worship. So if it is not fitting for us to associate anything with You, how would it be fitting for us to call Your servants to worship us besides You? This meaning is more majestic and greater than the first, so reflect upon it.

The point is: on both readings, this answer is from the angels and from whoever was worshipped besides Allah among His friends.

As for its being from the idols, it is not apparent.

It may be said: Allah, glorified is He, made them speak thereby, as a refutation of them, a rebuttal to them, and a disavowal of them, like His saying:

﴿When those who were followed disown those who followed﴾ [al-Baqara: 166].

And in another verse: ﴿We disown You; they did not used to worship us﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 63].

Then the worshipped mentioned the reason the worshippers abandoned belief in Allah, the Exalted, by their saying:

﴿But You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people ruined (būran)﴾ [al-Furqān: 18].

Ibn ʿAbbās said: You prolonged their lives, bestowed favors upon them, and widened their provision.

Al-Farrāʾ said: "But You gave them enjoyment with wealth and children until they forgot Your remembrance, and they were a people ruined" — that is, perishing, corrupt, overcome by wretchedness and abandonment. Al-Bawār means destruction and corruption; it is said: "bārat al-silʿa" (the merchandise became unsaleable) and "bārat al-mar'a" (the woman remained unmarried) when no one came to marry her.

Qatāda said: By Allah, no people forgot the remembrance of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, except that they were ruined and corrupted.

The meaning: "We did not lead them astray, but they went astray."

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿So they have denied you in what you say﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

That is, the worshipped denied you by your saying about them that they are gods and partners, or by your saying that they commanded you to worship them and called you to it.

It was said: the address is to the believers in this world: that is, these polytheists have denied you, O believers, in what you say, which Muḥammad (ﷺ) brought from Allah of monotheism and faith. The first is more apparent, and the context indicates it.

As for one who reads it with the letter of the third person (yaqūlūna), the meaning is: "they have denied you by their statement," then He said:

﴿So you are not able to avert (ṣarfan) nor to obtain help (naṣran)﴾ [al-Furqān: 19].

This is reporting their condition on that Day, and that they are not able to avert the punishment from themselves, nor to get help for themselves from Allah.

Ibn Zayd said: On the Day of Resurrection, when the creatures are gathered, a herald will call out: whoever was worshipped besides Allah, let him not help today whoever worshipped him, and the worshipper does not help his god:

﴿Rather, they will today be submissive﴾ [aṣ-Ṣāffāt: 26].

This is the condition of the servants of Satan on the day of meeting the Most Merciful. Woe to their bad condition when they are separated from the believers, when they hear the call:

﴿And separate yourselves today, O criminals. Did I not enjoin upon you, O children of Adam, that you not worship Satan? Indeed, he is to you a clear enemy. And that you worship Me; this is a straight path. And he had already led astray from among you a great multitude. Then did you not use reason?﴾ [Yā-Sīn: 59-62].

The commentary on the verse ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others﴾

﴿وَجَعَلْنا بَعْضَكم لِبَعْضٍ فِتْنَةً﴾

This applies to all of creation: some are tested by others. The messengers were tested by those to whom they were sent, through calling them to the truth and through patience with their harm, and through bearing the hardships of conveying the messages of their Lord. Those to whom the messengers were sent were tested by the messengers: will they obey them, support them, and believe them, or will they disbelieve in them, reject them, and fight them? The scholars were tested by the ignorant: will they teach them, advise them, and be patient in teaching, advising, and guiding them, and in what that entails? The ignorant were tested by the scholars: will they obey them and be guided by them? Rulers were tested by their subjects, and subjects by their rulers. The rich were tested by the poor, and the poor by the rich. The weak were tested by the strong, and the strong by the weak. Masters were tested by their followers, and followers by their masters. The owner was tested by his slave, and the slave by him. A man was tested by his wife, and his wife by him. Men were tested by women, and women by men. Believers were tested by disbelievers, and disbelievers by believers.

The enjoiners of good were tested by those they enjoin, and those enjoined were tested by them. For this reason, the poor and weak among the believers, who were followers of the messengers, became a trial for their rich and their leaders, who refused to believe after recognizing the truthfulness of the messengers, and said: ﴿Had it been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾ — meaning these people.

And they said to Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿Shall we believe you when the lowest of people follow you?﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 111].

He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And thus We tested some of them through others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?"﴾ [al-An'am: 53].

So when the noble, the chief, sees that the poor, humble one has preceded him to faith and following the Messenger, he becomes resentful and disdainful of accepting Islam, lest he become like him, and says: "Shall I accept Islam so that I and this lowly one are on equal footing?"

Al-Zajjaj said: A noble man might wish to embrace Islam, but refrains from it lest it be said that someone inferior to him embraced it before him, so he remains upon his disbelief, lest the Muslim have precedence over him in virtue.

Among the ways in which some people are a trial for others: the poor man says, "Why was I not like the rich man?"

The weak says, "Why was I not like the strong?"

The afflicted says, "Why was I not like the healthy?"

And the disbelievers said: ﴿We will not believe until we are given what was given to the messengers of Allah﴾ [al-An'am: 124].

Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning the disbelievers' trial by the poor emigrants, such as Bilal, Khabbab, Suhayb, Abu Dharr, Ibn Mas'ud, and 'Ammar. The disbelievers of Quraysh used to say: "Look at these who followed Muhammad, our clients and the lowest of us!"

Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said: "Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful." But you took them in mockery, until they made you forget My remembrance, and you used to laugh at them. Indeed, I have rewarded them today for their patience; indeed, they are the triumphant﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 109-111].

So He informed, glorified be He, that He rewarded them for their patience, as He said: ﴿And We have made some of you a trial for others. Will you be patient?﴾ [al-Furqan: 20].

Al-Zajjaj said: That is, "Will you be patient over the affliction? You have known what the patient have attained."

I say: Allah, glorified be He, joins trial with patience here, and in His saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried and then struggled and were patient﴾ [al-Nahl: 110].

There is no cure for one who has been afflicted by a trial like patience. If he is patient, the trial becomes a purification for him and a cleansing from sins, just as the furnace purges the dross from gold and silver.

Trial is thus the furnace of hearts and the touchstone of faith, and through it the truthful is distinguished from the liar. He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And We certainly tested those before them, and Allah will surely make evident those who are truthful and will surely make evident the liars﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 3].

Trial thus divides people into truthful and liar, believer and hypocrite, good and wicked. Whoever is patient through it, it becomes a mercy for him, and by his patience he is saved from a greater trial than it; whoever is not patient through it falls into a trial more severe than it.

Trial is inevitable in this world and the Hereafter, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Day they will be tormented in the Fire: "Taste your trial; this is what you used to seek to hasten"﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 13-14].

Thus the Fire is a trial for whoever was not patient through the trial of this world. Concerning the tree of Zaqqum He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We have made it a trial for the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Saffat: 63].

Qatadah said: When Allah mentioned this tree, the wrongdoers were tested by it. They said: "Is there a tree in the Fire, while the Fire consumes trees?" So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire﴾ [al-Saffat: 64].

So He informed them that its nourishment is from the Fire, that is, it is nourished by fire.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The tree of Zaqqum may be a plant of fire, made of a substance that fire does not consume. Likewise are the chains of the Fire, its shackles, its fetters, its scorpions, and its serpents. If they were as we know them, they would not survive in the Fire. Allah, the Exalted, has only pointed us to what is unseen to Him by what is seen to us, so the names agree in indication while the meanings differ. The same applies to what is in Paradise of its fruit, its furnishings, its trees, and all its implements.

The point is that this tree is a trial for them in this world, through their denial of it, and a trial for them in the Hereafter, through their eating from it.

Likewise, His informing that the number of angels assigned to the Fire is nineteen became a trial for the disbelievers. The enemy of Allah, Abu Jahl, said: "Does Muhammad frighten you with nineteen, while you are numerous? Can each hundred of you not overpower one of them, and then you come out of the Fire?"

Abu al-Asad said: "O assembly of Quraysh, when the Day of Resurrection comes, I will walk before you on the Sirat, and I will push ten of them with my right shoulder and nine with my left shoulder into the Fire, and we will proceed and enter Paradise."

So the mention of this number was a trial for them in this world, and a trial for them on the Day of Resurrection.

The disbeliever is tested by the believer in this world, just as the believer is tested by him. For this reason the believers asked their Lord not to make them a trial for the disbelievers, as the ḥanīfs (those who turn sincerely to the one God) said: ﴿Our Lord, upon You we have relied, and to You we have turned, and to You is the final return. Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the disbelievers﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4-5].

And the companions of Moses, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people﴾ [Yunus: 85].

Mujahid said: The meaning is: do not punish us by their hands, nor by a punishment from You, lest they say, "If these were upon the truth, this would not have befallen them."

Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is: do not let them prevail over us, lest they think they are upon the truth and be tested thereby.

Al-Farra' said: Do not let the disbelievers prevail over us, lest they see that they are upon the truth and I am upon falsehood.

Muqatil said: Do not restrict provision from us while extending it to them, for that would be a trial for them.

Allah, glorified be He, has informed that He has tested each of the two groups by the other, saying:

﴿And thus We tested some of them through others, that they might say: "Are these the ones upon whom Allah has bestowed favor from among us?"﴾

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿Is not Allah most knowing of who is grateful?﴾

The point is that Allah, glorified be He, tested the people of desires through beautiful forms, and tested those (the beautiful forms) through them. Each of the two kinds is a trial for the other. Whoever among them is patient through that trial is saved from what is greater than it, and whoever is struck by that trial falls into what is worse than it. If one remedies that through repentance and sincere advice, well; otherwise he is on the path of those who perished. For this reason the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him and his family, said:

"I have not left after me a trial more harmful to men than women."

Or as he said.

The servant in this abode is tested by his desires, his commanding self, his misleading and beautifying devil, his companions, and what he sees and witnesses, which his patience cannot withstand. Added to this are weak faith and certainty, a feeble heart, the bitterness of patience, the taste of immediate pleasure, the inclination of the soul toward the splendor of the worldly life, and the reward being deferred to another abode other than this one in which he was created and raised. So he is obligated to abandon his present, visible desire for an unseen matter he is commanded to believe in:

Indeed, by Allah, were it not that Allah makes His servant happy through His granting success, and Allah is more merciful to the servant,

Faith would never have firmly settled in his heart one day despite these hardships, though the matter is greater.

Nor would his soul have obeyed him in abandoning a desire, out of fear of a Fire whose embers blaze,

Nor would he have feared one day the station of his God over him, by the judgment of justice, for He does not wrong.

**(Benefit)**

The abandonment of the Qur'an (hajr al-Qur'an) takes several forms.

The first is abandoning its hearing, believing in it, and giving it attention.

The second is abandoning acting upon it and stopping at its permitted and forbidden matters, even if one recites it and believes in it.

The third is abandoning seeking its judgment and referring to it in matters of the foundations of religion (usul al-din) and its branches (furu'), while holding the belief that it does not yield certainty and that its proofs are merely verbal and do not produce knowledge.

The fourth is abandoning its contemplation (tadabbur) and understanding (tafahhum), and recognizing what the Speaker intended by it.

The fifth is abandoning seeking healing and cure through it for all diseases of the heart and their afflictions, so one seeks the cure of one's illness from other than it, and abandons treating oneself with it. All of this falls within His saying: ﴿And the Messenger says, "My Lord, indeed my people have taken this Qur'an as something abandoned."﴾

Although some forms of abandonment are lighter than others.

Similarly, the constriction (haraj) that lies in the breasts concerning it: sometimes it is a constriction about its being sent down and its being the truth from Allah; sometimes it is from the standpoint of its being spoken, or its being a created thing among the creatures of Allah, which inspired someone other than Him to speak it; sometimes it is from the standpoint of its sufficiency or lack thereof, and that it does not suffice the servants, but rather they are in need alongside it of rational reasoning (ma'qulat), analogies (aqisah), opinions (ara'), or political policies (siyasat); sometimes it is from the standpoint of its indication and what is meant by it, its apparent realities (haqa'iq) understood from it at the time of address, or it is intended to interpret them and take them out of their realities into strained, shared interpretations; and sometimes it is from the standpoint that those realities, even if intended, are established in the actual matter, or that one imagines they are intended for the sake of a contrived benefit. All of these have constriction in their breasts concerning the Qur'an, and they know this from their own souls and find it in their breasts. You will never find a innovator (mubtadi') in his religion except that there is constriction in his heart from the verses that contradict his innovation, just as you will never find a wicked oppressor except that there is constriction in his chest from the verses that stand between him and his desire.

So contemplate this meaning, then be content for yourself with whatever you wish.

(Section: On the blameworthiness of desire (hawa) and the attainment of hopes through opposing it)

Hawa (desire) is the inclination of the natural disposition toward what suits it. This inclination is created in a human being out of necessity for his survival, for were it not for his inclination toward food, drink and marriage, he would neither eat, drink nor marry. Thus desire impels him toward what he wants, just as anger repels from him what would harm him. Therefore desire should not be condemned absolutely nor praised absolutely, just as anger is neither blamed absolutely nor praised absolutely. What is blameworthy is only the excess of either of the two, namely what exceeds the attainment of benefits and the repelling of harms. Since most of those who obey their desire, their lust and their anger do not stop at the limit of what benefits them, the blame of desire, lust and anger is stated in general terms, because the prevalence of harm is general. Few are those who seek justice in this and stop at it, just as a perfectly balanced temperament is rare in every respect; rather, the dominance of one of the humors and qualities over it is inevitable. Thus the advisor's eagerness to balance the powers of lust and anger in every respect is a matter that is impossible to achieve except in the case of a few individuals of the world. For this reason, Allah the Exalted has not mentioned desire (hawa) in His Book except to condemn it, and likewise in the Sunnah it has come only as blameworthy, except what came qualified, such as his saying: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought." And it has been said: "Desire is a hidden ambush that cannot be trusted."

Al-Sha'bi said: It was named hawa because it casts its companion down (yahwi), and its unrestricted form calls to present pleasure without reflection on the consequence, and urges the attainment of appetites quickly, even if they are a cause of the greatest pains, both swiftly and later. For this world has a consequence before the consequence of the Hereafter.

Desire blinds its companion from observing this, while manliness (muruwwah), religion and intellect forbid a pleasure that leads to pain and an appetite that brings about regret. Each of them says to the soul when it wishes that: Do not do that. And obedience belongs to whichever prevails. Do you not see that the child prefers what he desires even if it leads him to destruction, because the restraining power of his intellect is weak? And one who has no religion prefers what he desires even if it leads him to his ruin in the Hereafter, because the restraining power of religion is weak? And one who has no manliness prefers what he desires even if it damages or destroys his manliness, because the restraining power of manliness is weak. How far is this from the saying of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him: "If I knew that cold water would damage my manliness, I would not drink it."

When the responsible person was tested with desire above all other animals, and since events occur to him at every moment, two judges were placed within him: the judge of intellect and the judge of religion. He was commanded to always refer the events of desire to these two judges and to submit to their ruling. He should train himself to repel desires whose consequences are safe, so that he may thereby train himself to abandon what its consequences harm. Let the discerning person know that those addicted to appetites come to a state in which they take no pleasure from them, and yet they cannot abandon them, because they have become for them like the livelihood they cannot do without. For this reason you see that the drunkard and the one addicted to intercourse take not a tenth of the pleasure from it that one who does it rarely takes, yet habit compels it, so he throws himself into ruin to attain what habit demands of him. Had the rust of desire departed from him, he would know that he has been wretched in the very place where he expected felicity, has grieved where he thought there was joy, and has been pained where he sought pleasure. He is like the bird deceived by a grain of wheat: he has neither obtained the grain nor escaped what he has fallen into.

If it is said: How can one who has fallen into this escape from it?

It is said: He can escape it, by the help of Allah and His granting him success, through several matters:

The first: the resolve of a free man who is jealous for himself and over himself.

The second: a draught of patience, by which he makes his soul patient over its bitterness at that hour.

The third: a strength of soul that encourages him to drink that draught. Courage is entirely an hour of patience, and the best life a servant attains is through his patience.

The fourth: his observing the good outcome of the consequence and the healing through that draught.

The fifth: his observing the pain that exceeds the pleasure of obeying his desire.

The sixth: his preserving his station with Allah the Exalted and in the hearts of His servants, which is better and more beneficial for him than the pleasure of conforming to desire.

The seventh: his preferring the pleasure of chastity, its dignity and its sweetness over the pleasure of disobedience.

The eighth: his joy at the defeat of his enemy, his subjugation of him, and his sending him back humiliated, enraged, grieved and distressed, since he did not attain his wish from him. Allah the Exalted loves that His servant should infuriate His enemy and enrage him, as Allah the Exalted said in His Mighty Book: "They tread no path that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they gain any gain from an enemy except that a righteous deed is recorded for them by it." And He said: "That He may enrage the disbelievers by them." And Allah the Exalted said: "Whoever emigrates in the way of Allah will find in the earth many a refuge and abundance," i.e., a place where he enrages the enemies of Allah. The sign of true love is to anger the enemies of the Beloved and to enrage them.

The ninth: reflecting that he was not created for desire, but was prepared for a great matter that he cannot attain except by disobeying desire, as it has been said:
"They have prepared you for a matter which, if you understood it, you would keep yourself above grazing with the herd."

The tenth: that he should not choose for himself that a dumb animal be better off than he. For the animal distinguishes by its nature between the places of what harms it and what benefits it, so it prefers the beneficial over the harmful. And the human being was given intellect for this very meaning. So if he does not distinguish by it between what harms him and what benefits him, or knows that yet prefers what harms him, the state of the dumb animal is better than his. This is shown by the fact that the beast obtains from the pleasure of food, drink and intercourse what a human being does not attain, with a pleasant life free of thought and worry. For this reason it is led to its slaughter while absorbed in its appetites, due to its lack of knowledge of consequences. A human being does not attain what the animal attains, because of the strength of preoccupying thought and the weakness of the instrument used, and other reasons. So if attaining the desired thing were a virtue, the human's share of it would not have been diminished, which is the essence of the world, while the animals' share was increased. In the furnishing of the human's share of intellect, knowledge and understanding there is a compensation for that.

The eleventh: that he should travel in his heart through the consequences of desire, and reflect on how many virtues his disobedience has caused to be lost, how many vices it has caused him to fall into, how many meals it has prevented from being eaten, how many pleasures it has made to be missed, how many appetites it has broken rank, bowed the head, disgraced a reputation, brought blame, caused humiliation and imposed a shame that water cannot wash away. But the eye of the one who follows desire is blind.

The twelfth: that the intelligent person should imagine the fulfilment of his aim from the one he desires, then imagine his state after the satisfaction of his need, what he has lost and what has come to him.
"The best of people is one who does not commit a cause until he discerns what its consequences will bring."

The thirteenth: that he should imagine that in the case of another person, imagining it fully, and then place himself in that same station. The judgment of a thing is the judgment of its like.

The fourteenth: that he should reflect on what his soul demands of him in this regard, and ask his intellect and religion about it; they will inform him that it is nothing. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "If one of you is taken with a woman, let him remember her ugliness." And this is better than the saying of Ahmad ibn al-Husayn:
"If the lover reflected on the end of the beauty that has captivated him, he would not have been captivated."
Because Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned the present, constant state, while the poet described a state appearing later.

The fifteenth: that he should be ashamed for his soul of the humiliation of obeying desire, for no one has ever obeyed his desire without finding in himself abasement. Let him not be deceived by the boasting and arrogance of the followers of desire, for they are the most abased of people inwardly, having combined the two branches of arrogance and humiliation.

The sixteenth: that he should weigh the safety of religion, honour, wealth and rank against attaining the sought pleasure, for there is absolutely no comparison between them. Let him know that it is among the most foolish of people to sell this for that.

The seventeenth: that he should be ashamed for his soul to be under the subjugation of his enemy. For when Satan sees in the servant weakness of resolve, lowness of ambition and inclination toward his desire, he covets him, overpowers him, bridles him with the bridle of desire and drives him wherever he wishes. And whenever he perceives in him strength of determination, nobility of soul and loftiness of aspiration, he does not covet him except by stealth and theft.

The eighteenth: that he should know that desire never mixes with anything without corrupting it. If it enters knowledge, it leads it out to innovation and misguidance, and its companion becomes among the people of desires. If it enters asceticism, it leads its companion to ostentation and opposition to the Sunnah. If it enters judgment, it leads its companion to injustice and turns him away from the truth. If it enters distribution, it moves it out of the division of justice into the division of oppression. If it enters appointment and dismissal, it leads its companion to betray Allah and the Muslims, since he appoints by his desire and dismisses by his desire. If it enters worship, it removes it from being obedience and nearness to Allah. Thus it corrupts whatever it accompanies.

The nineteenth: that he should know that Satan has no entrance into the son of Adam except through the gate of his desire. He circles around him seeking an entrance, until he corrupts his heart and his deeds, and finds no entry except through the gate of desire, and then he spreads within him like poison spreading through the limbs.

The twentieth: that Allah, glorified and exalted, made desire opposed to what He sent down to His Messenger, and made following it the counterpart of following His messengers. He divided people into two kinds: followers of revelation and followers of desire. This is frequent in the Qur'an, such as His saying: "But if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their desires." And His saying: "And if you were to follow their desires after the knowledge that has come to you..." and their likes.

The twenty-first: that Allah, glorified and exalted, likened the followers of desire to the basest of animals in form and in meaning. He likened them to the dog at times, as in His saying: "But he clung to the earth and followed his desire; so his likeness is the likeness of the dog." And to donkeys at other times, as in His saying: "As if they were startled donkeys fleeing from a lion." And He transformed their forms into the forms of apes and swine at other times.

The twenty-second: that the follower of desire is not fit to be obeyed, nor to be an imam or one who is followed. For Allah, glorified and exalted, removed him from the imamate and forbade obeying him. As for his removal, Allah, glorified and exalted, said to His friend Ibrahim: "Indeed I will make you an imam for the people." He said: "And from my offspring?" He said: "My covenant does not attain the wrongdoers." That is, My covenant of imamate does not attain one who is a wrongdoer. And everyone who follows his desire is a wrongdoer, as Allah the Exalted said: "Rather, those who did wrong followed their desires without knowledge." As for the prohibition of obeying him, it is due to His saying: "And do not obey one whose heart We have made heedless of Our remembrance, who follows his desire, and whose affair has become excess."

The twenty-third: that Allah, glorified and exalted, made the follower of desire in the position of the idol-worshipper, and so said: "Have you seen one who has taken his desire as his god?" in two places in His Book.

Al-Hasan said: It is the hypocrite, who does not desire anything except that he mounts it. And he also said: The hypocrite is a slave of his desire; he does not desire anything except that he does it.

The twenty-fourth: that desire is the enclosure of Hell surrounding it on all sides, so whoever falls into it falls into the Fire, as in the two Sahihs from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Paradise is surrounded by hardships, and the Fire is surrounded by desires."

In al-Tirmidhi, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, traced to the Prophet: "When Allah created Paradise, He sent Jibril to it, saying: Look at it and at what I have prepared for its people in it. He came and looked at it and at what Allah had prepared for its people in it. He returned to Him and said: By Your might, no one among Your servants will hear of it without entering it. So He commanded that it be veiled with hardships, and said: Return to it and look at it. He returned, and it had been veiled with hardships. He said: By Your might, I feared that no one would enter it. He said: Go to the Fire and look at it and at what I have prepared for its people in it. He came and looked at it and at what Allah had prepared for its people in it, and behold, parts of it were piled upon parts. He said: By Your might, no one will hear of it and enter it. So He commanded that it be surrounded with desires, and said: Return and look at it. He returned to it, and behold, it had been surrounded with desires. He returned to Him and said: By Your might, I feared that no one would be saved from it."

al-Tirmidhi said: This is a hadith that is ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.

The twenty-fifth: that one who follows desire is feared to be stripped of faith while he is unaware. It has been established from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "None of you truly believes until his desire is subordinate to what I have brought." And it is authentically reported from him that he said: "What I fear most for you are the desires of error in your bellies and your private parts, and the misleading desires."

The twenty-sixth: that following desire is among the destroyers. He said: There are three saving matters and three destroying matters. As for the saving ones: fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, in secret and in public; speaking the truth in contentment and in anger; and moderation in wealth and poverty. As for the destroying ones: a desire that is followed, a miserliness that is obeyed, and a man's self-admiration.

The twenty-seventh: that opposing desire brings the servant strength in his body, his heart and his tongue. One of the early generation said: The one who conquers his desire is stronger than the one who conquers a city alone. And in the authentic hadith traced to the Prophet: "The strong man is not the one who overthrows others, but the strong man is the one who controls himself at the time of anger." And whenever one trains himself to oppose his desire, he gains strength upon his strength.

The twenty-eighth: that the most abundant in manliness are the most opposed to their desires. Mu'awiyah said: Manliness is abandoning appetites and disobeying desire. So following desire paralyses manliness, and opposing it revives it.

The twenty-ninth: that there is not a day but desire and intellect wrestle within their companion. Whichever of them prevails over its companion drives it out and gains control, and the ruling belongs to it. Abu al-Darda' said: When a man rises in the morning, his desire and his deed are gathered together. If his deed follows his desire, his day is a day of evil; and if his desire follows his deed, his day is a day of goodness.

The thirtieth: that Allah, glorified and exalted, made error and following desire companions, and made correctness and opposing desire companions, as one of the early generation said: If two matters become unclear to you and you do not know which of them is more rightly guided, then oppose the nearer of them to your desire, for error is most likely to occur in following desire.

The thirty-first: that desire is a disease and its cure is opposing it. One of the knowers said: If you wish, I will tell you of your disease, and if you wish, I will tell you of your cure. Your disease is your desire, and your cure is abandoning your desire and opposing it.

Bishr al-Hafi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: All affliction is in your desire, and all healing is in your opposing it.

The thirty-second: that the struggle against desire, if it is not greater than the struggle against the disbelievers, is not less than it. A man said to al-Hasan al-Basri, may Allah have mercy on him: O Abu Sa'id, which jihad is the best? He said: Your jihad against your desire. And I heard our shaykh say: The struggle against the self and desire is the root of the struggle against the disbelievers and hypocrites, for one cannot fight them until he first struggles against his self and his desire, so that he may go out to them.

The thirty-third: that desire is disorder, and opposing it is a protective regimen, and one who exceeds in disorder and neglects the regimen is feared to be overcome by his disease. Abd al-Malik ibn Qurayb said: I passed by a Bedouin who had a severe eye inflammation, his tears flowing down his cheeks. I said: Will you not wipe your eyes? He said: The physician has forbidden me that, and there is no good in one who, when restrained, is not restrained, and when commanded, does not obey. I said: Do you not desire anything? He said: Yes, but I observe the regimen. The people of the Fire were overcome by their desire over their regimen, so they perished.

The thirty-fourth: that following desire closes the doors of success upon the servant and opens upon him the doors of abandonment. You see him constantly saying that if Allah had granted success, it would have been such-and-such; yet he has himself blocked the paths of success by following his desire. Al-Fudayl ibn Iyad said: Whoever is seized by desire and the pursuit of appetites, the sources of success are cut off from him.

Some scholars said: Disbelief lies in four things: anger, lust, desire and fear. Then he said: I have seen two of them: a man who became angry and killed his mother, and a man who fell in love and became a Christian. One of the early generation was circumambulating the House, and he looked at a beautiful woman, so he walked beside her and then said:
"I love the love of religion, and pleasures please me; how can I have the love of pleasures and the love of religion?"
She said: Leave one of them and you will attain the other.

The thirty-fifth: that whoever supports his desire, his intellect and judgment are corrupted for him, for he has betrayed Allah regarding his intellect, and so He corrupts it for him. This is the way of Allah, glorified and exalted, with everyone who betrays Him in any matter: He corrupts it for him.

Al-Mu'tasim once said to one of his companions: O so-and-so, when desire prevails, judgment departs. I heard a man say to our shaykh: If a man betrays in assessing dirhams, Allah takes from him the knowledge of assessing them, or he forgets it. The shaykh said: Likewise, whoever betrays Allah and His Messenger in matters of knowledge.

The thirty-sixth: that whoever gives his soul latitude in following desire, constricts it in its grave and on its day of return; and whoever constricts it by opposing desire, widens it in its grave and its return. Allah the Exalted has pointed to this in His saying: "And He rewarded them for what they endured with a garden and silk." So since in patience, which is restraining the soul from desire, there is roughness and constriction, He recompensed them for that with the softness of silk and the spaciousness of Paradise.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani, may Allah have mercy on him, said regarding this verse: "He rewarded them for what they endured," i.e., for their patience against appetites.

The thirty-seventh: following desire (al-hawa) throws the servant down from rising on the Day of Resurrection to strive alongside those who are saved, just as it threw his heart down in this world from keeping company with them. Muhammad ibn Abi al-Ward said: "Indeed, God, Mighty and Majestic, has a day from whose evil no one escapes except one who submits to his desire. And though the slowest of the fallen to rise on the Day of Resurrection is the one felled by his lust. When minds ran in the fields of seeking, the most abundant in their share were those who pursued them in proportion to the patience and intellect that accompanied them. The intellect is a mine, and thought is a pickaxe."

The thirty-eighth: following desire dissolves resolve and weakens it, while opposing it strengthens and fortifies it. Resolve is the mount of the servant by which he travels to God and the Last Abode. So when the mount is disabled, the traveler is near to being cut off. It was said to Yahya ibn Mu'adh, "Who among people is most firm in resolve?" He said, "The one who overcomes his desire." Khalaf ibn Khalifa entered upon Sulayman ibn Habib ibn al-Muhallab, and with him was a slave-girl called al-Badr, among the most beautiful of people in face. Sulayman said to him, "How do you see this slave-girl?" He replied, "May God make the Amir righteous, my eyes have never seen anything more beautiful than her." Sulayman said to him, "Take her by the hand." He said, "I would not distress the Amir with her, for I have seen how greatly he admires her." Sulayman said, "Woe to you! Take her despite my great admiration for her, so that my desire may know that I am its conqueror." He took her by the hand and went out, saying:

> He has favoured me, given to me, and preferred me
> Without my asking, Sulayman [did so].
> He gave me al-Badr, a maiden of beautiful qualities,
> Though al-Badr was never given to man or jinn.
> I shall never forget his favour, ever,
> Until a grave and shrouds cover me.

The thirty-ninth: the likeness of one who rides desire is like the likeness of one who rides a fierce, stubborn, unbridled horse, for it is likely that his horse will throw him during its gallop or carry him to destruction. Some of the knowers said: "The swiftest of mounts to Paradise is renunciation of this world, and the swiftest of mounts to the Fire is love of appetites. Whoever sits firmly upon the back of his desire, it will hasten him to the valley of ruin." Another said: "The noblest of scholars is one who flees with his religion from this world and finds it hard to subdue himself to desire." 'Ata said: "Whoever his desire overcomes, his intellect and his patience will betray him, and he will be disgraced."

The fortieth: tawhid (monotheism) and following desire are opposites, for desire is an idol, and every servant has an idol in his heart according to his desire. God sent His messengers only to break idols and worship Him alone, without partner. God, glorified be He, does not intend merely the breaking of physical idols and the abandonment of the idols in the heart; rather, what is intended is breaking them out of the heart first. Al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Mutawwi'i said: "The idol of every person is his desire. Whoever breaks it by opposing it earns the name of chivalry (fututwa)."

Consider the words of the Friend (al-Khalil, Ibrahim, peace be upon him) to his people: ﴿What are these statues to which you are devoted?﴾ See how you find it applies to the statues that the heart desires, devotes itself to, and worships besides God. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Have you seen him who takes as his god his own desire? Would you then be a guardian over him? Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are not but like livestock; rather, they are further astray in way.﴾

The forty-first: opposing desire keeps disease away from the heart and body, while following it brings about diseases of the heart and body. All the diseases of the heart come from following desire, and if you examine the diseases of the body, you will find that most of them come from preferring desire over what ought to be abandoned.

The forty-second: the root of enmity, evil, and envy that occurs among people is following desire. Whoever opposes his desire gives rest to his heart, body, and limbs, so he rests and gives rest to others. Abu Bakr al-Warraq said: "When desire prevails, the heart is darkened; when it is darkened, the chest is constricted; when the chest is constricted, character is corrupted; and when character is corrupted, people hate him, and he hates them. So consider what arises from mutual hatred: evil, enmity, the abandonment of rights, and other things."

The forty-third: God, glorified and exalted be He, placed in the servant both desire and intellect, and whichever of them manifests, the other is concealed. As Abu Ali al-Thaqafi said: "Whoever his desire overcomes, his intellect is hidden from him. So consider the outcome of one whose intellect is concealed from him and its opposite prevails over him." Ali ibn Sahl, may God have mercy on him, said: "Intellect and desire contend with one another. Success (tawfiq) accompanies intellect, and abandonment (khudhlan) accompanies desire, while the soul (nafs) stands between them. Whichever prevails, the soul is with it."

The forty-fourth: God, glorified be He, made the heart the king of the limbs, the mine of its knowledge, love, and servitude, and tested it with two authorities, two armies, two helpers, and two provisions. Truth, renunciation, and guidance are one authority, whose helpers are the angels and whose army is sincerity and devotion, and avoiding desire and falsehood. The other authority is that of the devils, whose army and provisions are following desire. The soul stands between the two armies. The army of falsehood does not advance upon the heart except through its gap and its side. The soul then conspires against the heart and sides with its enemy against it, so the reversal falls upon it. It is the soul that gives its enemy his provisions from within, opens the gate of the city for him, so he enters, takes possession, and abandonment befalls the heart.

The forty-fifth: the most hostile enemy of a person is his own devil and his desire, and the most sincere friend to him is his intellect and the counselling angel. When he follows his desire, he gives his hand to his enemy, surrenders to him, makes him rejoice over him, and grieves his friend and ally. This itself is the very essence of severe affliction, the depth of misery, evil destiny, and the gloating of enemies.

The forty-sixth: every servant has a beginning and an end. Whoever's beginning is following desire, his end will be humiliation, abasement, deprivation, and affliction, in proportion to what he followed of his desire. Indeed, that end becomes for him a torment in his heart, as the poet said:

> Desires that were, for their people in youth, a torment,
> Became in old age a torment.

So if you reflect on the state of everyone in a wretched, shameful condition, you will see that his beginning was going along with his desire and preferring it over his intellect. Whoever's beginning was opposing his desire and obeying the caller to his right guidance, his end will be honour, nobility, wealth, and standing with God and with people. Abu Ali al-Daqqaq said: "Whoever masters his lust in his youth, God, the Exalted, will honour him in his old age." It was said to al-Muhallab ibn Abi Sufra, "By what did you attain what you attained?" He said, "By obeying prudence and disobeying desire." This is in the beginning and end of this world. As for the Hereafter, God, glorified be He, made Paradise the end for one who opposed his desire, and the Fire the end for one who followed his desire.

The forty-seventh: desire is a bondage in the heart, a fetter on the neck, and a shackle on the foot, and its follower is a captive to every master of evil. Whoever opposes it is freed from its bondage, becomes free, has the yoke removed from his neck and the shackle from his foot, and becomes like a man who is wholly owned by one master after having been a man in whom there were quarrelling partners.

> How many a concealed one whom desire has disgraced,
> So his covering was stripped away and he was exposed.
> The owner of desire is a slave; but when
> He overcomes desire, he becomes a king.

Ibn al-Mubarak said:

> Among affliction, and affliction has a sign:
> That you not see yourself turning back from your desire.
> The servant is a slave of the soul in its appetites,
> While the free man is sated at times and hungry at others.

The forty-eighth: opposing desire places the servant in a station where, if he swore by God, God would fulfil it for him. He is given manifold, many times over, what he missed of his desire. He is like one who turned away from a piece of dung and was given a pearl in exchange. The follower of desire loses from his immediate and deferred interests, and from pleasant living, what has no comparison at all with what he gained of his desire.

Reflect on the extension of the hand of Yusuf the Truthful, peace be upon him, and his tongue, his foot, and his self after he came out of prison, when he restrained himself from what was forbidden.

Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi said: "I saw Sufyan al-Thawri, may God have mercy on him, in a dream, and I asked him, 'What did God do with you?' He said, 'Nothing happened except that I was placed in my grave until I stood before God, blessed and exalted be He, and He reckoned with me with an easy reckoning. Then He commanded that I be taken to Paradise. As I was wandering among its trees and rivers, hearing neither sound nor movement, I suddenly heard a caller saying, "Sufyan ibn Sa'id." I said, "Sufyan ibn Sa'id!" He said, "Do you remember that you once preferred God, the Mighty and Majestic, over your desire?" I said, "Yes, by God!" Then the scattered gifts (nithar) seized me from every side.'"

Abd al-Razzaq said: "Abu Ja'far sent the Khashshabin (wood-men) when he went out to Mecca, saying, 'If you find Sufyan, crucify him.' They came and set up the wood, and he was sought, and his head was in the lap of al-Fudayl. His companions said to him, 'Fear God, the Mighty and Majestic, and do not let the enemies gloat over us.' So he advanced to the curtains of the Ka'ba, took hold of them with his hand, and said, 'I am free of him if Abu Ja'far enters it.' Then he died before Abu Ja'far entered Mecca." Reflect on the outcome of opposing desire and how it raised him to this station.

The forty-ninth: opposing desire brings about the honour of this world and the honour of the Hereafter, outward honour and inward honour, while following it lowers the servant in this world and the Hereafter, and humiliates him outwardly and inwardly. When God gathers the people on one level plain, a herald will call out: "Let the people of the gathering know who are the people of nobility today! Let the God-fearing stand up!" They will rise to the place of honour, while the followers of desire will have their heads bowed in the place of standing, in the heat of desire, its sweat, and its pain. Those, however, will be in the shade of the Throne.

The fiftieth: if you reflect on the seven whom God, the Mighty and Majestic, will shade under His Throne on the day when there is no shade but His shade, you will find that they attained that shade only by opposing desire. The mighty ruling leader cannot be just except by opposing his own desire. The young man who prefers the worship of God over the call of his youth could not do so had he not opposed his desire. The man whose heart is attached to the mosques was moved to this only by opposing the desire that called him to the places of pleasures. The one who gives charity in secret, so that his left hand does not know what his right hand gives, could not do so had he not overcome his desire. The one who was called by a beautiful, noble woman and feared God, the Mighty and Majestic, and opposed his desire. The one who remembered God in seclusion and his eyes overflowed from fear of Him, was brought to that only by opposing his desire. Thus the heat, the sweat, and the severity of the Standing on the Day of Resurrection will have no way over them. As for the followers of desire, heat and sweat will have reached them at every degree, and they will be awaiting, after this, entry into the prison of desire.

So God, glorified and exalted be He, is asked to protect us from the desires of our souls that command evil, and to make our desire follow what He loves and is pleased with. He is over all things capable, and worthy of responding.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 25, verse 44:

The five senses have forms and spirits, and the spirits of the senses are the heart's share and portion of them.

Among people are those whose hearts have no share of them except the share that animals have of them. Such a person is in the rank of those animals. Between him and them lies only the first degree of humanity. For this reason, Allah, glorified is He, likened those people to cattle, and even made them more astray. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Or do you think that most of them hear or understand? They are only like livestock; rather, they are even more astray in the way﴾ [al-Furqan: 44].

For this reason, Allah negated from the disbelievers hearing, sight and intellect.

This is either because they did not benefit from them, so they were placed in the position of the non-existent,

or because the negation was directed at the hearing, sight and perception of their hearts.

This is why that becomes apparent to them when the realities of matters are revealed, like the words of the people of the Blaze: ﴿Had we been listening or understanding, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze﴾ [al-Mulk: 10].

(Subtle point)

Abu Ja'far al-Baqir said: "By Allah, He did not limit Himself to likening them to cattle, but made them more astray than them."

(Section)

He likened most people to cattle. The common factor between the two kinds is equality in not accepting guidance and not submitting to it. He made the majority more astray in the way than cattle, because a beast is guided by its driver, so it follows the path and does not swerve from it to the right or the left. The majority are called by the messengers, who show them the way, yet they do not respond, are not guided, and do not distinguish between what harms them and what benefits them. Cattle distinguish between plants and paths that harm them, avoiding them, and what benefits them, preferring it. Allah, exalted is He, did not create for cattle hearts with which to understand, nor tongues with which to speak, while He gave these people such things. Then they did not benefit from the intellects, hearts, tongues, hearing and sight that He had given them. Therefore they are more astray than beasts. Indeed, one who does not find the right direction and the path when a guide to it is present is more astray and in a worse state than one who does not find it where no guide is with him.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 25, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 3):**

The meaning of the verse is to draw attention to this striking sign of the power of the Lord, glorified is He, and to the wonders of His creation that point to Him. The meaning is: "Look at how your Lord extended the shadow. The shadow is what lies before the zenith, and the shade (*fay')* is what comes after it. He, glorified is He, extended it and spread it out at sunrise, when it is at its longest. He made the sun a proof of it, for it is the sun that makes it appear and clarifies it. Then, as the sun rises higher, a part of the shadow contracts, and it keeps decreasing little by little until it reaches its limit. When the sun begins to decline toward the west, the shadow expands again gradually until it returns to its state at sunrise."

For this reason, the time of midday (*zawal*) is known by the shadow reaching its shortest length. When it begins to lengthen again after its shortest length, the midday has been confirmed. Had God willed, He would have made it constant, always in one state, not moving by increase or decrease. So the shadow is one of the proofs of the Creator, glorified is He.

**(Section)**

He, may He be exalted, informed that He spread the shadow and extended it, and that He made it move following the movement of the sun. Had He willed, He would have made it still and unmoving, either by making the object that casts it still, or by some other cause.

Then He informed that He contracted it after spreading it, by a small contraction, bit by bit, not all at once.

This is among the greatest of His signs, indicating the magnitude of His power and the perfection of His wisdom.

He, glorified is He, therefore urged the contemplation of His craftsmanship, power and wisdom in this single item of His creation. Had our Lord willed, He would have made the shadow adhere to the base of whatever casts it, such as a mountain, a building, a tree or other things, and then its people would not have benefited from it. The full benefit of it follows from its extension, its spreading out, and its shifting from place to place.

In its extension and spreading, and then its gradual contraction, there are benefits and advantages that cannot be concealed or counted.

Had it been constantly still, or had it contracted all at once, the affairs of the world and its interests would have been disrupted, both by it and by the sun. So the extension of the shadow and its gradual contraction are a necessary consequence of the movement of the sun, in accordance with what He determined for the interests of the world.

In the sun's indication of the shadows there is what allows the times of the prayers to be known, and how much of the day has passed and how much remains.

In its movement and shifting there is what cools whatever the heat of the sun has touched, and benefits animals, trees and plants. So it is among the signs that point to Him.

There is another interpretation of the verse: that He extended the shadow when He built the heaven like a stretched dome and spread out the earth beneath it, so the dome cast its shadow upon the earth.

Had He willed, He would have made it still and fixed in that state. Then He created the sun and set it up as a proof of that shadow, so it follows the sun in its movement, increasing and decreasing with it, extending and contracting. It is subordinate to the sun in the way the thing indicated is subordinate to its indicator.

There is another interpretation: that what is meant is the contraction of the shadow at the establishment of the Hour, by the seizing of its causes, which are the bodies that cast shadows. Thus the verse mentions its annihilation by the annihilation of its causes, just as it mentioned its origination by the origination of its causes.

His saying, *"Then We contracted it toward Us,"* seems to indicate this.

His saying, *"a gradual contraction,"* resembles His saying, *"That is a gathering that is easy for Us."*

His saying, *"We contracted it,"* in the past tense, does not contradict this, as in His saying, *"The command of God has come."*

The correct interpretation of the verse is the first one.

**[Section on direct witnessing (*ma'ayana*)]**

Shaykh al-Islam said: "Chapter on direct witnessing (*ma'ayana*)." God, may He be exalted, said: *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"* (Al-Furqan: 45).

I say: *Ma'ayana* is a form of *mu'ayana*, derived from *'iyan* (direct sight), and its origin is seeing with the eye. It is said: "He witnessed him (*'ayanahu*)" when his eye fell upon him, just as it is said: "He spoke to him face to face (*shafahahu*)" when he spoke to him directly, and "he faced him (*wajahahu*)" when he confronted him face to face. And this is impossible in this world for a human being to attain.

As for His saying, *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"*, the seeing falls upon the act of extending the shadow itself, not upon the One who extended it, glorified is He. As He said: *"Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?"* (Nuh: 15), and His saying: *"Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the People of the Elephant?"* (Al-Fil: 1). Here He placed the seeing upon the act itself. In His saying, *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"*, He placed it in the wording upon Him, glorified is He, while what is meant is His act of extending the shadow. This is clear Arabic whose meaning is plain, neither ambiguous nor unclear, as was said about al-'Uzza:

*"Your disbelief today, not your glorification; for I have seen God has humiliated you."*

This is common in their speech. They say: "I saw God do such and such," and what is meant is "I saw His act." So the witnessing and the seeing fall upon the object (of the act), not upon the essence of the Agent, nor His attribute, nor the act subsisting in Him.

**[Section on the types of direct witnessing]**

The author of *al-Manazil* (*Manazil al-Sa'irin*, by al-Ansari al-Harawi) said: "Direct witnessing is of three kinds. The first: witnessing by the eyes. The second: witnessing by the eye of the heart, which is knowing the very thing as it is described, with a knowledge that removes doubt and is not mixed with bewilderment. The third: witnessing by the eye of the spirit, which witnesses the Truth with pure direct vision. Spirits were purified and honored with permanence so that they might witness the radiance of the Presence, behold the splendor of majesty, and draw hearts to the sanctuary of the Presence."

The Shaykh assigned witnessing to the eye, the heart and the spirit, and gave a ruling for each kind of witnessing.

As for the witnessing of the eye: it is seeing a thing directly, either by the impression of the image of the seen object upon the seeing faculty, according to those who hold the theory of impression; or by the connection of a ray extending from the eye to the seen object, according to those who hold the theory of rays; or by the particular relation and connection between the eye and the seen object, according to many of the theologians. These three opinions are not free from error and correctness, and the truth is something other than them. God, glorified is He, placed in the eye a faculty of sight, just as He placed in the ear a faculty of hearing, in the nose a faculty of smell, and in the tongue a faculty of speech and a faculty of taste. These are faculties that God, glorified is He, deposited in these organs, and He made a bond between them and between (their objects), and He made for them causes from outside, and impediments that prevent their rulings. All that they mentioned, such as impression, facing, ray, relation and connection, is a cause and a condition, while the effective agent is the faculty subsisting in the organ. The purpose here is not to discuss this question, for the intended matter is something else.

As for the witnessing of the heart: it is the unveiling of the form of the known object to it, such that its relation to the heart is like the relation of the seen object to the eye. God, glorified is He, made the heart able to see and to be blind, just as the eye sees and is blind. He, may He be exalted, said: *"For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded"* (Al-Hajj: 46). The heart sees and hears, and it is blinded and deafened, and its blindness and deafness are more severe than the blindness and deafness of sight.

As for what the later scholars of this group affirm concerning this third kind, namely the seeing of the spirit, its hearing, its will and its rulings, which are more particular than the rulings of the heart: their belief is that the spirit is other than the soul (*nafs*) and the heart.

There is no doubt that there are certain known matters here: the body; its spirit which subsists in it; the heart in which the faculties are seen, and in the rest of the animal; and the natural disposition (*gharizah*), which is the rational faculty whose locus is the heart. Its relation to the heart is like the relation of the faculty of sight to the eye and the faculty of hearing to the ear. For this reason, that faculty is called "heart," just as the faculty of sight is called "sight." He, may He be exalted, said: *"Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart"* (Qaf: 37), and He did not mean the physical shape of the heart, for that is in everyone, but He meant the faculty and the natural disposition deposited in it.

The spirit (*ruh*) is what carries the body and all these faculties, and the body and its faculties have no stability except by it. And it has, according to its attachment to each locus, a name and a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of sight, it is called "sight," and it has a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of hearing, it is called "hearing," and it has a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of reason, which is the heart, it is called "heart," and it has a ruling specific to it there. In all of that, it is a spirit.

So the faculty of sight, the rational faculty, the faculty of hearing and the faculty of speech are a seeing spirit, a hearing spirit, a rational spirit and a speaking spirit. In reality, it is this rational, understanding, perceiving, loving, knowing thing which moves the body, which is the locus of address, command and prohibition. It is one thing having multiple attributes according to its objects. It is called a soul at rest (*nafs mutma'innah*), a self-reproaching soul (*nafs lawwamah*), and a commanding soul (*nafs ammarah*). It is not three souls in essence and reality, but it is one soul having multiple attributes.

They use the word "soul" to refer to blameworthy character and attributes. They say: "So-and-so has a soul," and "So-and-so has no soul." It is known that if his soul departed from him he would die, but they mean his detachment from the blameworthy attributes of the soul.

The verifiers among them say: when the soul becomes refined and abandons vices, it becomes a spirit. It is known that it has not been annihilated, and that a spirit that did not exist before is created in its place, but the blameworthy attributes have been annihilated from it, and praiseworthy attributes have taken their place, so it was called a spirit.

This is a mere terminology. Otherwise, God, glorified and exalted is He, called it "soul" (*nafs*) in the Qur'an in all its states: commanding, self-reproaching and at rest. He, may He be exalted, said: *"God takes the souls at the time of their death"* (Al-Zumar: 42). This includes all the souls of the servants, even the prophets.
