And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called it "spirit" in an absolute sense, whether it was that of a believer or a disbeliever, righteous or wicked, as in his saying: "When the spirit is taken, the sight follows it," and his saying: "God takes our spirits wherever He wills, and returns them wherever He wills," and his saying (ﷺ), in the hadith about the taking of the spirit and its description: "If he was a believer, such and such, and if he was a disbeliever, such and such." Thus he called the one taken a "spirit," just as God called it a "soul" in His Book. The one taken and the one who has died are one thing, not three and not two. When it is taken, all the faculties follow it, the intellect and what is below it, because it was the carrier of all of them and their vehicle.

Having known this, direct witnessing is of two kinds: the witnessing of sight and the witnessing of insight. The witnessing of sight is the falling of sight upon the seen object itself or its external image, like seeing the image of a form in a mirror or water. The witnessing of insight is the falling of the rational faculty upon the knowledge-image that corresponds to the external thing, so its perception of it is like the eye's perception of the external form. The authority of this inner perception may grow strong, to the point that its judgment prevails. The rational faculty's retention of what it perceives may grow strong, to the point that it becomes absorbed in it. Then the judgment of the heart overcomes the judgment of sensation and observation, and it takes control of hearing and sight, so that he sees it and hears its address externally, while it is only in the soul and the mind. But because of the dominance of contemplation, the strength of retention, and the firm establishment of the judgment of the heart and its dominance over the faculties, it becomes as though it were seen by the eye and heard by the ear, such that the perceiver has no doubt and no suspicion whatsoever about it, and accepts no reproach.

The reality of the matter is that all of this is evidence and knowledge-examples following the belief. So that which is perceived by the eye of the heart and the spirit is only an indicator pointing to the Reality, and it is not the Reality itself. The witness of the light of the majesty of the Essence in the heart of the servant is not the very light of the Essence, before which the heavens and the earth cannot stand. For if it had appeared to them, they would have been crushed to dust, and would have suffered what the mountain suffered. Likewise, the witness of the light of greatness in the heart is only the light of veneration and reverence, not the light of the essence of the One who is venerated, Lord of Majesty and Honor.

The people have nothing but the witnesses, the knowledge-examples, and the subtleties which are the fruit of the heart's nearness to the Lord, its intimacy with Him, its absorption in His love and remembrance, and the dominion of the knowledge of Him over it. The Lord, blessed and exalted, is beyond all that, transcendent and holy above human access to His Essence, or the lights of His Essence, or His attributes, or the lights of His attributes. What exists are the witnesses that stand in the heart of the servant, just as there stands in his heart a witness of the Hereafter, Paradise and Hell, and what God has prepared for their people.

This is what 'Abd Allah ibn Haram al-Ansari found on the day of Uhud, when he said: "Wah! The scent of Paradise! I find its scent, by God, beyond Uhud!" From this is His (ﷺ) saying: "When you pass by the gardens of Paradise, graze in them." They said: "What are the gardens of Paradise?" He said: "The circles of remembrance." And from it is his saying: "Between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise." So it is a garden for the people of knowledge and faith, because of what stands in their hearts of the witnesses of Paradise, until it is as though it is before their eyes. When a hypocrite sits there, that place is not a garden of the gardens of Paradise for him. And from this is his saying (ﷺ): "Paradise is under the shade of the swords."

So action is only based on the witnesses, and according to the witness of the servant his action is shaped.

We will now, with God's help and guidance, point out the witnesses, in a manner by which the reality of the matter may be known.

The first of the witnesses (shāhid, a perception or insight that arises in the heart) of one who travels toward God and the Last Abode is that there arises in him a witness from this world and its lowliness, the scarcity of its loyalty, the abundance of its harshness, the baseness of its partners, and the swiftness of its passing. He sees its people and its lovers lying slain around it. It has deceived them and tormented them with every kind of torment, and made them taste its most bitter drink. It made them laugh a little and weep a long time. It gave them to drink from the cups of its poison after the cups of its wine, so they became intoxicated with its love and died through its forsaking.

When this witness from it arises in the servant, his heart departs from it and journeys in search of the Last Abode. Then there arises in his heart a witness from the Hereafter and its permanence, and that it is truly the Life, so its people do not depart from it or move away from it. Rather, it is the abode of settlement, the resting place of men, and the end of the journey. The world, in comparison to it, is as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «The world, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing but what one of you would dip his finger into the sea, and then see what it brings back.»

One of the Successors (tābi'īn, the generation after the Companions) said: "The world, compared to the Hereafter, is less than a single grain among the mountains of the world."

Then there arises in his heart a witness from the Fire, its blazing and kindling, the depth of its bottom, the severity of its heat, and the great torment of its people. He sees them being driven toward it with black faces and blue eyes, with chains and shackles around their necks. When they reach it, its gates are opened in their faces, and they witness that dreadful sight, their hearts torn apart by regret and sorrow. ﴿And the guilty will see the Fire and will be certain that they are to fall into it, and they will find no way to escape from it.﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. So the witness of faith shows him this, while they are being pushed toward it. The call comes from the Lord of the worlds: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned.﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. Then it is said to them: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or is it that you do not see? Burn in it, and whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you; you are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ [al-Tur: 14-16]. The witness of faith sees them in the boiling water, dragged on their faces, and in the Fire, burning like wood. ﴿For them there is a bed of Hell, and above them coverings of it.﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. How evil is that covering, and how evil is that bed! If they call for help from the severity of thirst, ﴿they will be given water like molten brass that scalds the faces.﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. When they drink it, it cuts their bowels within their bellies and melts what is in their stomachs. Their drink is boiling water and their food is the zaqqum. ﴿It shall not be decreed for them that they die, nor shall its torment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one. And they will cry out therein: "Our Lord, bring us out, and we shall do righteous deeds other than those we used to do." Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would remember to remember? And the warner came to you. So taste it, for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾ [Fatir: 36-37].

When this witness arises in the heart of the servant, he sheds sins, disobedience, and the pursuit of desires. He puts on the garments of fear and caution. His heart becomes fertile from the rain of his eyelids. Every calamity that befalls him in matters other than his religion and his heart becomes easy for him.

In proportion to the strength of this witness, he will be after it (further) from disobedience and transgressions. This witness melts away the impurities and destructive matter from his heart, ripens them, and then expels them. So the heart finds the sweetness of well-being and its joy.

After that there arises in him a witness from Paradise, and what God has prepared for its people therein, things which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have not occurred to the heart of any human being, let alone what God has described to His servants through the tongue of His Messenger of the detailed bliss that suffices for the highest kinds of delight: of foods and drinks, garments and forms, joy and happiness. So there arises in his heart the witness of an abode in which God has placed the lasting, everlasting bliss in its entirety. Its soil is musk, its pebbles are pearls, its buildings are bricks of gold and silver, and its reeds are of pearls. Its drink is sweeter than honey, more fragrant than musk, cooler than camphor, and more delicious than ginger. Its women, if the face of one of them were to appear in this world, would outshine the light of the sun. Their clothing is silk of sundus and istabraq. Their servants are youths like scattered pearls. Their fruit is everlasting, neither cut off nor forbidden. The couches are raised high. Their food is the flesh of birds of whatever they desire, and their drink is wine with which there is no harm, nor are they made drunk by it. Their greenery is fruit of whatever they choose. Their companions are the dark-eyed maidens, like hidden pearls. They recline on couches, and in those gardens they are delighted, and therein is whatever the souls desire and whatever the eyes delight in, and they abide therein forever.

When there is joined to this witness the witness of the Day of Increase (yawm al-mazīd), the sight of the Face of the Lord, may His majesty be exalted, and hearing His speech from Him without intermediary, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, exalted is He, has looked down upon them from above and said: "O people of Paradise, peace be upon you." Then He recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]» Then He withdraws from them, and His mercy and blessing remain upon them in their abodes.

When this witness is joined to the witnesses that came before it, the heart then travels toward its Lord faster than the winds in their courses, and it does not turn aside on its path to the right or the left.

Beyond all this there is another witness, in which these witnesses vanish, and in which the servant is absorbed away from them all. It is the witness of the majesty of the Lord, exalted is He, His beauty and perfection, His might and sovereignty, His self-subsistence (qayyūmiyya), His elevation above His Throne, His speech through His books and the words of His creation, and His address to His angels and prophets.

When he witnesses Him with his heart, he witnesses One Self-Subsistent, Dominant over His servants, established upon His Throne, alone in the governance of His kingdom, commanding and forbidding, sending His messengers and sending down His books, who is pleased and angry, who rewards and punishes, who gives and withholds, who exalts and abases, who loves and hates, who has mercy when asked for mercy, who forgives when asked for forgiveness, who gives when asked, who answers when called upon, who pardons when pardon is sought. He is greater than everything, mightier than everything, more powerful than everything, more knowing than everything, and wiser than everything. Even if the powers of all creatures were concentrated in one of them, and then all of them possessed that power, and then these powers were compared to the power of a gnat in comparison to the power of a lion, and if the beauty of all creation were concentrated in one of them, and then all of them possessed that beauty, and then this were compared to the beauty of the Lord, exalted is He, it would be less than a weak lamp compared to the disk of the sun. And if the knowledge of the first and the last were concentrated in one man, and then all creation possessed that same attribute, and then this were compared to the knowledge of the Lord, exalted is He, it would be like the peck of a sparrow in the sea. The same applies to all His attributes, such as His hearing and His sight, and all the descriptors of His perfection. He hears the clamour of voices in their differing languages, with their varied needs. His hearing is not distracted by one sound from another, the questions do not confuse Him, and He is not wearied by the insistence of those who press Him. Whether one speaks secretly or openly is the same to Him; the secret is open to Him and the unseen is witnessed by Him. He sees the crawling of a black ant on a smooth rock on a dark night, and sees the sinews of its veins and the channels of nourishment in its limbs. He places the heavens on one of His fingers, the earth on one finger, the mountains on one finger, the trees on one finger, and the water on one finger. He grasps His heavens in one of His hands and the earths in the other. The seven heavens in His palm are like a mustard seed in the palm of a servant. And even if all creation, from the first of them to the last, were to stand in one row, they would not encompass God, Mighty and Majestic. If He were to unveil the veil from His face, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His gaze reached.

When this witness arises in the servant's heart, the preceding witnesses dissolve in it without being annihilated. Rather, dominance and supremacy belong to this witness, and all the witnesses are gathered within it. The one who has this witness has a special path and journey that is not shared by others who are heedless of this, or who have only a general knowledge.

The companion of this witness travels toward God in his waking and sleeping, in his movement and stillness, in his breaking of the fast and his fasting. He has a concern, and people have their concern; he is in one valley and people are in another valley.

﻿Two friends of mine, by God, I am not of you two, if he who knows of the family of Layla appears to me.

The point is that direct witnessing, unveiling, and vision in this abode occur only through witnesses and scientific examples, which is the Sublime Parable that He, glorified is He, mentioned in three places in His Book: in Surat al-Nahl, Surat al-Rum, and Surat al-Shura. It is what arises in the hearts of His worshippers and lovers and those who turn toward Him, from this witness. It is what motivates them to worship, love, fear, and turning in repentance. Their variation in it has no limit at either end. Each of them has a known station that he does not exceed. The greatest of people in this regard is one who acknowledges that he cannot count the praises of Him, glorified is He, and that He is above what those who praise Him praise Him for, and above what those who commend Him commend Him for, as it has been said:

"The eulogists have not reached toward You with any praise, though they have been lavish; what is in You is greater."

"To You is all praise, a praise without beginning or end, and God is most knowing of praise."

The purity of the heart and its freedom from blameworthy attributes, base desires, and its emptying and clearing of attachment to other than God, glorified is He, is the throne (kursī) of this witness, upon which it sits, and the seat in which it is established. So it is forbidden for a heart that is polluted with corruption, bad character, and blameworthy qualities, attached to base desires, that this witness should arise in it or that it should be among its people.

"Purify your heart from other than us and come to us, for our threshold is lawful to every one who is pure. And patience is the talisman for the treasure of our meeting; whoever unlocks this talisman wins its treasure."

When the sun of tawhīd (the oneness of God) rises, and its rays touch the spirits and its light reaches the insights, the darknesses of the self and the natural temperament are revealed by it, and the spirits move in search of Him to whom nothing is like, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. The heart then travels through the wilderness of the command and alights at the stations of servanthood, station after station. It moves from one act of worship to another, while remaining fixed upon one object of worship. The witnesses of the attributes never cease to abide in its heart, awakening it when it sleeps, reminding it when it is heedless, driving it when it travels, and keeping it when it sits. If a witness of lordship and self-subsistence arises in its heart, it sees that the whole affair belongs to God, and that no one has any share of it with Him: ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold it, and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him. He is the Mighty, the Wise. O people, remember the blessing of God upon you. Is there any creator other than God who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? There is no god but He, so how are you turned away? And if God touches you with harm, none can remove it but He; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty. He bestows it upon whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: "God." Say: "Have you considered what you call upon besides God? If God intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?" Say: "God is sufficient for me; in Him the trusting put their trust."﴾ ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?" They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then remember?" Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?" They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then fear God?" Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of everything, who protects and against whom no protection is given, if you know?" They will say: "To God." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2-89].

If there stands in his heart a witness of divinity, he sees in that witness the command and the prohibition, the prophethoods, the books and the laws, love and good pleasure, dislike and hatred, and reward and punishment. He witnesses the command descending from the One who is established upon His Throne ('arsh), and the deeds of the servants ascending to Him and being presented before Him. He repays the good among them in this abode and, in the Hereafter, with radiance and joy. And He turns to whatever deeds were not according to His command and law, and makes them scattered dust.

If there stands in his heart a witness of mercy, he sees all existence standing in this attribute. The One whose attribute it is has encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge. His mercy extends to where His knowledge extends. So He established Himself upon His Throne by His mercy, so that it might embrace everything, just as His Throne has encompassed everything.

If there stands in his heart a witness of might, greatness, majesty and dominance, then it has another matter.

Thus it is with all the witnesses of the attributes. What we have mentioned is only the slightest indication of them. Unveiling (kashf), direct vision ('iyan) and contemplation (mushahadah) never go beyond the witnesses at all. So let us return to explaining his words.

As for his words, regarding the second degree: "It is the direct viewing of the eye of the heart (mu'ayanat 'ayn al-qalb)." He means by it knowing a thing according to its description, which it has in external reality in every respect. This is impossible with regard to knowing what is in the Hereafter of created things, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in the Hereafter except the names." So how can one know the Lord of the earth and the heavens? The utmost of knowledge is that one's knowledge of Him conforms to His description, either in a general or a detailed manner, detailed in some respects.

His words: "Knowledge that cuts off doubt and is not mixed with bewilderment." This is true. For knowledge, when doubt or bewilderment mixes with it, is not sound knowledge, just as sight of the eye, if it were mixed with such, would not be complete sight. So knowledge is that which cuts off doubt, hesitation and whispering.

His words: "The third direct viewing is the eye of the spirit (ruh), which beholds the Truth with pure beholding."

If by "the Truth" he means the opposite of falsehood, that is, it beholds what is true, in such a way that it is unveiled to it as the visible is unveiled to sight, then it is correct. If by "the Truth" he means the Lord, blessed and exalted, then unless his words are understood as referring to the strength of certainty, increase of faith, and the descent of the spirit into the station of excellence (ihsan), it is false. For the Lord, blessed and exalted, is not beheld in this abode by any eye or spirit. Rather, the knowledge-based likeness is the portion of the spirit and heart, as has preceded.

His words: "The spirits were only purified and honored with permanence, so that they may behold the radiance of the Presence (hadrah), and witness the splendor of might, and draw hearts to the precincts (fina') of the Presence."

He means: the spirits were created for permanence, not for annihilation. This is the truth, and only a small group of people opposed it, from among the people of atheism (ilhad), who say that spirits perish with the perishing of bodies, because they are a power of the bodily powers and an accident of its accidents.

These are two groups. One denies the bodily resurrection (ma'ad al-abdan). The second acknowledges the bodily resurrection and says that God, mighty and majestic, restores the powers of the body and its accidents, and among them the spirit, which perishes with the perishing of bodies. So for both groups there is no spirit subsisting in itself, which dwells with the body and departs from it, connects to it and separates from it.

As for the truth on which the messengers and their followers agreed: these spirits endure after their bodies depart. They do not perish and are not annihilated, and they are blessed or punished in the barzakh (intermediate state). When the Day of Resurrection comes, they are returned to their bodies, and they are blessed or punished along with them. They are not destroyed or annihilated.

So his words: "And the spirits, when they are purified and honored with permanence, to behold the radiance of the Presence," he means the pure and purified spirits. In another copy the reading is "to converse with (lituna'iya) the radiance of the Presence," but the first is more evident and more closely connected to the chapter he titled "the chapter of direct viewing." By "the Presence" is meant the Divine Presence, and by "radiance" (sana') the light that gleams. God, exalted, said: ﴿The flash of His lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. The direct viewing of that is only in the Hereafter, while the one who views here is the light of knowledge and the knowledge-based likeness.

His words: "And witness the splendor of might." Splendor (bahaʾ) in the language means beauty, as al-Jawhari said. From it one says: "bahiya al-rajul" (the man became beautiful), with the vowel kasra, and also "bahuwa," so he is "bahiyy" (beautiful).

Might ('izzah) is used with three meanings: might of strength, might of invulnerability (imtina'), and might of subjugation (qahr). The Lord, blessed and exalted, possesses perfect might in all three considerations. From the first one says "'azza ya'azzu" with fatha in the imperfect; from the second, "'azza ya'izzu" with kasra; and from the third, "'azza ya'uzzu" with damma. They gave the strongest vowels to the strongest meanings, the lightest to the lightest, and the middle to the middle. This might necessarily entails unity (wahdaniyyah), since association diminishes might. It necessarily entails the attributes of perfection, since association contradicts the perfection of might. It necessarily entails the negation of its opposites, and it necessarily entails the negation of any other's likeness to Him in any of these.

So the spirit beholds, by the strength of its knowledge and faith, the splendor of might, its majesty and its greatness. This direct viewing is the result of sound belief that corresponds to the truth in reality, received from the niche of revelation. So no one who stands with the measures of the philosophers, the disputation of the theologians, and the imaginings of the Sufis can hope for it.

His words: "And draw hearts to the precincts of the Presence." The word (fina') is with a kasra on the fa', meaning the side (janib) of the Presence. He means: the spirits, because of the strength of their seeking and the intensity of their longing, drive the hearts and pull them there. For the seeking and movement of the spirit are stronger than the seeking and movement of the heart, just as its direct viewing is more complete than the heart's.

In sum, the rulings of the spirit, according to them, are above the rulings of the heart and more specific than them.

The point is: when the spirit beholds the Truth, it draws all the powers and the heart to its presence, and the heart follows it in submission without resistance. This contrasts with the heart drawing (the body), for the limbs may resist it to some degree and refuse some things with aversion. But as for the spirit's drawing, there is no resistance with it and no refusal.

And success is from God.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 25, verses 45–46 (part 1 of 3):**

The meaning of the verse is to draw attention to this striking sign of the power of the Lord, glorified is He, and to the wonders of His creation that point to Him. The meaning is: "Look at how your Lord extended the shadow. The shadow is what lies before the zenith, and the shade (*fay')* is what comes after it. He, glorified is He, extended it and spread it out at sunrise, when it is at its longest. He made the sun a proof of it, for it is the sun that makes it appear and clarifies it. Then, as the sun rises higher, a part of the shadow contracts, and it keeps decreasing little by little until it reaches its limit. When the sun begins to decline toward the west, the shadow expands again gradually until it returns to its state at sunrise."

For this reason, the time of midday (*zawal*) is known by the shadow reaching its shortest length. When it begins to lengthen again after its shortest length, the midday has been confirmed. Had God willed, He would have made it constant, always in one state, not moving by increase or decrease. So the shadow is one of the proofs of the Creator, glorified is He.

**(Section)**

He, may He be exalted, informed that He spread the shadow and extended it, and that He made it move following the movement of the sun. Had He willed, He would have made it still and unmoving, either by making the object that casts it still, or by some other cause.

Then He informed that He contracted it after spreading it, by a small contraction, bit by bit, not all at once.

This is among the greatest of His signs, indicating the magnitude of His power and the perfection of His wisdom.

He, glorified is He, therefore urged the contemplation of His craftsmanship, power and wisdom in this single item of His creation. Had our Lord willed, He would have made the shadow adhere to the base of whatever casts it, such as a mountain, a building, a tree or other things, and then its people would not have benefited from it. The full benefit of it follows from its extension, its spreading out, and its shifting from place to place.

In its extension and spreading, and then its gradual contraction, there are benefits and advantages that cannot be concealed or counted.

Had it been constantly still, or had it contracted all at once, the affairs of the world and its interests would have been disrupted, both by it and by the sun. So the extension of the shadow and its gradual contraction are a necessary consequence of the movement of the sun, in accordance with what He determined for the interests of the world.

In the sun's indication of the shadows there is what allows the times of the prayers to be known, and how much of the day has passed and how much remains.

In its movement and shifting there is what cools whatever the heat of the sun has touched, and benefits animals, trees and plants. So it is among the signs that point to Him.

There is another interpretation of the verse: that He extended the shadow when He built the heaven like a stretched dome and spread out the earth beneath it, so the dome cast its shadow upon the earth.

Had He willed, He would have made it still and fixed in that state. Then He created the sun and set it up as a proof of that shadow, so it follows the sun in its movement, increasing and decreasing with it, extending and contracting. It is subordinate to the sun in the way the thing indicated is subordinate to its indicator.

There is another interpretation: that what is meant is the contraction of the shadow at the establishment of the Hour, by the seizing of its causes, which are the bodies that cast shadows. Thus the verse mentions its annihilation by the annihilation of its causes, just as it mentioned its origination by the origination of its causes.

His saying, *"Then We contracted it toward Us,"* seems to indicate this.

His saying, *"a gradual contraction,"* resembles His saying, *"That is a gathering that is easy for Us."*

His saying, *"We contracted it,"* in the past tense, does not contradict this, as in His saying, *"The command of God has come."*

The correct interpretation of the verse is the first one.

**[Section on direct witnessing (*ma'ayana*)]**

Shaykh al-Islam said: "Chapter on direct witnessing (*ma'ayana*)." God, may He be exalted, said: *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"* (Al-Furqan: 45).

I say: *Ma'ayana* is a form of *mu'ayana*, derived from *'iyan* (direct sight), and its origin is seeing with the eye. It is said: "He witnessed him (*'ayanahu*)" when his eye fell upon him, just as it is said: "He spoke to him face to face (*shafahahu*)" when he spoke to him directly, and "he faced him (*wajahahu*)" when he confronted him face to face. And this is impossible in this world for a human being to attain.

As for His saying, *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"*, the seeing falls upon the act of extending the shadow itself, not upon the One who extended it, glorified is He. As He said: *"Have you not seen how God created seven heavens in layers?"* (Nuh: 15), and His saying: *"Have you not considered how your Lord dealt with the People of the Elephant?"* (Al-Fil: 1). Here He placed the seeing upon the act itself. In His saying, *"Have you not considered your Lord, how He extended the shadow?"*, He placed it in the wording upon Him, glorified is He, while what is meant is His act of extending the shadow. This is clear Arabic whose meaning is plain, neither ambiguous nor unclear, as was said about al-'Uzza:

*"Your disbelief today, not your glorification; for I have seen God has humiliated you."*

This is common in their speech. They say: "I saw God do such and such," and what is meant is "I saw His act." So the witnessing and the seeing fall upon the object (of the act), not upon the essence of the Agent, nor His attribute, nor the act subsisting in Him.

**[Section on the types of direct witnessing]**

The author of *al-Manazil* (*Manazil al-Sa'irin*, by al-Ansari al-Harawi) said: "Direct witnessing is of three kinds. The first: witnessing by the eyes. The second: witnessing by the eye of the heart, which is knowing the very thing as it is described, with a knowledge that removes doubt and is not mixed with bewilderment. The third: witnessing by the eye of the spirit, which witnesses the Truth with pure direct vision. Spirits were purified and honored with permanence so that they might witness the radiance of the Presence, behold the splendor of majesty, and draw hearts to the sanctuary of the Presence."

The Shaykh assigned witnessing to the eye, the heart and the spirit, and gave a ruling for each kind of witnessing.

As for the witnessing of the eye: it is seeing a thing directly, either by the impression of the image of the seen object upon the seeing faculty, according to those who hold the theory of impression; or by the connection of a ray extending from the eye to the seen object, according to those who hold the theory of rays; or by the particular relation and connection between the eye and the seen object, according to many of the theologians. These three opinions are not free from error and correctness, and the truth is something other than them. God, glorified is He, placed in the eye a faculty of sight, just as He placed in the ear a faculty of hearing, in the nose a faculty of smell, and in the tongue a faculty of speech and a faculty of taste. These are faculties that God, glorified is He, deposited in these organs, and He made a bond between them and between (their objects), and He made for them causes from outside, and impediments that prevent their rulings. All that they mentioned, such as impression, facing, ray, relation and connection, is a cause and a condition, while the effective agent is the faculty subsisting in the organ. The purpose here is not to discuss this question, for the intended matter is something else.

As for the witnessing of the heart: it is the unveiling of the form of the known object to it, such that its relation to the heart is like the relation of the seen object to the eye. God, glorified is He, made the heart able to see and to be blind, just as the eye sees and is blind. He, may He be exalted, said: *"For indeed, it is not the eyes that are blinded, but it is the hearts within the breasts that are blinded"* (Al-Hajj: 46). The heart sees and hears, and it is blinded and deafened, and its blindness and deafness are more severe than the blindness and deafness of sight.

As for what the later scholars of this group affirm concerning this third kind, namely the seeing of the spirit, its hearing, its will and its rulings, which are more particular than the rulings of the heart: their belief is that the spirit is other than the soul (*nafs*) and the heart.

There is no doubt that there are certain known matters here: the body; its spirit which subsists in it; the heart in which the faculties are seen, and in the rest of the animal; and the natural disposition (*gharizah*), which is the rational faculty whose locus is the heart. Its relation to the heart is like the relation of the faculty of sight to the eye and the faculty of hearing to the ear. For this reason, that faculty is called "heart," just as the faculty of sight is called "sight." He, may He be exalted, said: *"Indeed, in that is a reminder for whoever has a heart"* (Qaf: 37), and He did not mean the physical shape of the heart, for that is in everyone, but He meant the faculty and the natural disposition deposited in it.

The spirit (*ruh*) is what carries the body and all these faculties, and the body and its faculties have no stability except by it. And it has, according to its attachment to each locus, a name and a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of sight, it is called "sight," and it has a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of hearing, it is called "hearing," and it has a ruling specific to it there. When it is attached to the locus of reason, which is the heart, it is called "heart," and it has a ruling specific to it there. In all of that, it is a spirit.

So the faculty of sight, the rational faculty, the faculty of hearing and the faculty of speech are a seeing spirit, a hearing spirit, a rational spirit and a speaking spirit. In reality, it is this rational, understanding, perceiving, loving, knowing thing which moves the body, which is the locus of address, command and prohibition. It is one thing having multiple attributes according to its objects. It is called a soul at rest (*nafs mutma'innah*), a self-reproaching soul (*nafs lawwamah*), and a commanding soul (*nafs ammarah*). It is not three souls in essence and reality, but it is one soul having multiple attributes.

They use the word "soul" to refer to blameworthy character and attributes. They say: "So-and-so has a soul," and "So-and-so has no soul." It is known that if his soul departed from him he would die, but they mean his detachment from the blameworthy attributes of the soul.

The verifiers among them say: when the soul becomes refined and abandons vices, it becomes a spirit. It is known that it has not been annihilated, and that a spirit that did not exist before is created in its place, but the blameworthy attributes have been annihilated from it, and praiseworthy attributes have taken their place, so it was called a spirit.

This is a mere terminology. Otherwise, God, glorified and exalted is He, called it "soul" (*nafs*) in the Qur'an in all its states: commanding, self-reproaching and at rest. He, may He be exalted, said: *"God takes the souls at the time of their death"* (Al-Zumar: 42). This includes all the souls of the servants, even the prophets. And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called it "spirit" in an absolute sense, whether it was that of a believer or a disbeliever, righteous or wicked, as in his saying: "When the spirit is taken, the sight follows it," and his saying: "God takes our spirits wherever He wills, and returns them wherever He wills," and his saying (ﷺ), in the hadith about the taking of the spirit and its description: "If he was a believer, such and such, and if he was a disbeliever, such and such." Thus he called the one taken a "spirit," just as God called it a "soul" in His Book. The one taken and the one who has died are one thing, not three and not two. When it is taken, all the faculties follow it, the intellect and what is below it, because it was the carrier of all of them and their vehicle.

Having known this, direct witnessing is of two kinds: the witnessing of sight and the witnessing of insight. The witnessing of sight is the falling of sight upon the seen object itself or its external image, like seeing the image of a form in a mirror or water. The witnessing of insight is the falling of the rational faculty upon the knowledge-image that corresponds to the external thing, so its perception of it is like the eye's perception of the external form. The authority of this inner perception may grow strong, to the point that its judgment prevails. The rational faculty's retention of what it perceives may grow strong, to the point that it becomes absorbed in it. Then the judgment of the heart overcomes the judgment of sensation and observation, and it takes control of hearing and sight, so that he sees it and hears its address externally, while it is only in the soul and the mind. But because of the dominance of contemplation, the strength of retention, and the firm establishment of the judgment of the heart and its dominance over the faculties, it becomes as though it were seen by the eye and heard by the ear, such that the perceiver has no doubt and no suspicion whatsoever about it, and accepts no reproach.

The reality of the matter is that all of this is evidence and knowledge-examples following the belief. So that which is perceived by the eye of the heart and the spirit is only an indicator pointing to the Reality, and it is not the Reality itself. The witness of the light of the majesty of the Essence in the heart of the servant is not the very light of the Essence, before which the heavens and the earth cannot stand. For if it had appeared to them, they would have been crushed to dust, and would have suffered what the mountain suffered. Likewise, the witness of the light of greatness in the heart is only the light of veneration and reverence, not the light of the essence of the One who is venerated, Lord of Majesty and Honor.

The people have nothing but the witnesses, the knowledge-examples, and the subtleties which are the fruit of the heart's nearness to the Lord, its intimacy with Him, its absorption in His love and remembrance, and the dominion of the knowledge of Him over it. The Lord, blessed and exalted, is beyond all that, transcendent and holy above human access to His Essence, or the lights of His Essence, or His attributes, or the lights of His attributes. What exists are the witnesses that stand in the heart of the servant, just as there stands in his heart a witness of the Hereafter, Paradise and Hell, and what God has prepared for their people.

This is what 'Abd Allah ibn Haram al-Ansari found on the day of Uhud, when he said: "Wah! The scent of Paradise! I find its scent, by God, beyond Uhud!" From this is His (ﷺ) saying: "When you pass by the gardens of Paradise, graze in them." They said: "What are the gardens of Paradise?" He said: "The circles of remembrance." And from it is his saying: "Between my house and my pulpit is a garden from the gardens of Paradise." So it is a garden for the people of knowledge and faith, because of what stands in their hearts of the witnesses of Paradise, until it is as though it is before their eyes. When a hypocrite sits there, that place is not a garden of the gardens of Paradise for him. And from this is his saying (ﷺ): "Paradise is under the shade of the swords."

So action is only based on the witnesses, and according to the witness of the servant his action is shaped.

We will now, with God's help and guidance, point out the witnesses, in a manner by which the reality of the matter may be known.

The first of the witnesses (shāhid, a perception or insight that arises in the heart) of one who travels toward God and the Last Abode is that there arises in him a witness from this world and its lowliness, the scarcity of its loyalty, the abundance of its harshness, the baseness of its partners, and the swiftness of its passing. He sees its people and its lovers lying slain around it. It has deceived them and tormented them with every kind of torment, and made them taste its most bitter drink. It made them laugh a little and weep a long time. It gave them to drink from the cups of its poison after the cups of its wine, so they became intoxicated with its love and died through its forsaking.

When this witness from it arises in the servant, his heart departs from it and journeys in search of the Last Abode. Then there arises in his heart a witness from the Hereafter and its permanence, and that it is truly the Life, so its people do not depart from it or move away from it. Rather, it is the abode of settlement, the resting place of men, and the end of the journey. The world, in comparison to it, is as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «The world, compared to the Hereafter, is nothing but what one of you would dip his finger into the sea, and then see what it brings back.»

One of the Successors (tābi'īn, the generation after the Companions) said: "The world, compared to the Hereafter, is less than a single grain among the mountains of the world."

Then there arises in his heart a witness from the Fire, its blazing and kindling, the depth of its bottom, the severity of its heat, and the great torment of its people. He sees them being driven toward it with black faces and blue eyes, with chains and shackles around their necks. When they reach it, its gates are opened in their faces, and they witness that dreadful sight, their hearts torn apart by regret and sorrow. ﴿And the guilty will see the Fire and will be certain that they are to fall into it, and they will find no way to escape from it.﴾ [al-Kahf: 53]. So the witness of faith shows him this, while they are being pushed toward it. The call comes from the Lord of the worlds: ﴿Stop them, for they are to be questioned.﴾ [al-Saffat: 24]. Then it is said to them: ﴿This is the Fire which you used to deny. Is this magic, or is it that you do not see? Burn in it, and whether you endure it or do not endure it, it is the same for you; you are only being recompensed for what you used to do.﴾ [al-Tur: 14-16]. The witness of faith sees them in the boiling water, dragged on their faces, and in the Fire, burning like wood. ﴿For them there is a bed of Hell, and above them coverings of it.﴾ [al-A'raf: 41]. How evil is that covering, and how evil is that bed! If they call for help from the severity of thirst, ﴿they will be given water like molten brass that scalds the faces.﴾ [al-Kahf: 29]. When they drink it, it cuts their bowels within their bellies and melts what is in their stomachs. Their drink is boiling water and their food is the zaqqum. ﴿It shall not be decreed for them that they die, nor shall its torment be lightened for them. Thus do We recompense every ungrateful one. And they will cry out therein: "Our Lord, bring us out, and we shall do righteous deeds other than those we used to do." Did We not give you a life long enough for whoever would remember to remember? And the warner came to you. So taste it, for the wrongdoers have no helper.﴾ [Fatir: 36-37].

When this witness arises in the heart of the servant, he sheds sins, disobedience, and the pursuit of desires. He puts on the garments of fear and caution. His heart becomes fertile from the rain of his eyelids. Every calamity that befalls him in matters other than his religion and his heart becomes easy for him.

In proportion to the strength of this witness, he will be after it (further) from disobedience and transgressions. This witness melts away the impurities and destructive matter from his heart, ripens them, and then expels them. So the heart finds the sweetness of well-being and its joy.

After that there arises in him a witness from Paradise, and what God has prepared for its people therein, things which no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and which have not occurred to the heart of any human being, let alone what God has described to His servants through the tongue of His Messenger of the detailed bliss that suffices for the highest kinds of delight: of foods and drinks, garments and forms, joy and happiness. So there arises in his heart the witness of an abode in which God has placed the lasting, everlasting bliss in its entirety. Its soil is musk, its pebbles are pearls, its buildings are bricks of gold and silver, and its reeds are of pearls. Its drink is sweeter than honey, more fragrant than musk, cooler than camphor, and more delicious than ginger. Its women, if the face of one of them were to appear in this world, would outshine the light of the sun. Their clothing is silk of sundus and istabraq. Their servants are youths like scattered pearls. Their fruit is everlasting, neither cut off nor forbidden. The couches are raised high. Their food is the flesh of birds of whatever they desire, and their drink is wine with which there is no harm, nor are they made drunk by it. Their greenery is fruit of whatever they choose. Their companions are the dark-eyed maidens, like hidden pearls. They recline on couches, and in those gardens they are delighted, and therein is whatever the souls desire and whatever the eyes delight in, and they abide therein forever.

When there is joined to this witness the witness of the Day of Increase (yawm al-mazīd), the sight of the Face of the Lord, may His majesty be exalted, and hearing His speech from Him without intermediary, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: «While the people of Paradise are in their bliss, a light shines upon them. They raise their heads, and behold, the Lord, exalted is He, has looked down upon them from above and said: "O people of Paradise, peace be upon you." Then He recited His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace, a word from a Lord, Most Merciful.﴾ [Ya-Sin: 58]» Then He withdraws from them, and His mercy and blessing remain upon them in their abodes.

When this witness is joined to the witnesses that came before it, the heart then travels toward its Lord faster than the winds in their courses, and it does not turn aside on its path to the right or the left.

Beyond all this there is another witness, in which these witnesses vanish, and in which the servant is absorbed away from them all. It is the witness of the majesty of the Lord, exalted is He, His beauty and perfection, His might and sovereignty, His self-subsistence (qayyūmiyya), His elevation above His Throne, His speech through His books and the words of His creation, and His address to His angels and prophets.

When he witnesses Him with his heart, he witnesses One Self-Subsistent, Dominant over His servants, established upon His Throne, alone in the governance of His kingdom, commanding and forbidding, sending His messengers and sending down His books, who is pleased and angry, who rewards and punishes, who gives and withholds, who exalts and abases, who loves and hates, who has mercy when asked for mercy, who forgives when asked for forgiveness, who gives when asked, who answers when called upon, who pardons when pardon is sought. He is greater than everything, mightier than everything, more powerful than everything, more knowing than everything, and wiser than everything. Even if the powers of all creatures were concentrated in one of them, and then all of them possessed that power, and then these powers were compared to the power of a gnat in comparison to the power of a lion, and if the beauty of all creation were concentrated in one of them, and then all of them possessed that beauty, and then this were compared to the beauty of the Lord, exalted is He, it would be less than a weak lamp compared to the disk of the sun. And if the knowledge of the first and the last were concentrated in one man, and then all creation possessed that same attribute, and then this were compared to the knowledge of the Lord, exalted is He, it would be like the peck of a sparrow in the sea. The same applies to all His attributes, such as His hearing and His sight, and all the descriptors of His perfection. He hears the clamour of voices in their differing languages, with their varied needs. His hearing is not distracted by one sound from another, the questions do not confuse Him, and He is not wearied by the insistence of those who press Him. Whether one speaks secretly or openly is the same to Him; the secret is open to Him and the unseen is witnessed by Him. He sees the crawling of a black ant on a smooth rock on a dark night, and sees the sinews of its veins and the channels of nourishment in its limbs. He places the heavens on one of His fingers, the earth on one finger, the mountains on one finger, the trees on one finger, and the water on one finger. He grasps His heavens in one of His hands and the earths in the other. The seven heavens in His palm are like a mustard seed in the palm of a servant. And even if all creation, from the first of them to the last, were to stand in one row, they would not encompass God, Mighty and Majestic. If He were to unveil the veil from His face, the glories of His face would burn away whatever of His creation His gaze reached.

When this witness arises in the servant's heart, the preceding witnesses dissolve in it without being annihilated. Rather, dominance and supremacy belong to this witness, and all the witnesses are gathered within it. The one who has this witness has a special path and journey that is not shared by others who are heedless of this, or who have only a general knowledge.

The companion of this witness travels toward God in his waking and sleeping, in his movement and stillness, in his breaking of the fast and his fasting. He has a concern, and people have their concern; he is in one valley and people are in another valley.

﻿Two friends of mine, by God, I am not of you two, if he who knows of the family of Layla appears to me.

The point is that direct witnessing, unveiling, and vision in this abode occur only through witnesses and scientific examples, which is the Sublime Parable that He, glorified is He, mentioned in three places in His Book: in Surat al-Nahl, Surat al-Rum, and Surat al-Shura. It is what arises in the hearts of His worshippers and lovers and those who turn toward Him, from this witness. It is what motivates them to worship, love, fear, and turning in repentance. Their variation in it has no limit at either end. Each of them has a known station that he does not exceed. The greatest of people in this regard is one who acknowledges that he cannot count the praises of Him, glorified is He, and that He is above what those who praise Him praise Him for, and above what those who commend Him commend Him for, as it has been said:

"The eulogists have not reached toward You with any praise, though they have been lavish; what is in You is greater."

"To You is all praise, a praise without beginning or end, and God is most knowing of praise."

The purity of the heart and its freedom from blameworthy attributes, base desires, and its emptying and clearing of attachment to other than God, glorified is He, is the throne (kursī) of this witness, upon which it sits, and the seat in which it is established. So it is forbidden for a heart that is polluted with corruption, bad character, and blameworthy qualities, attached to base desires, that this witness should arise in it or that it should be among its people.

"Purify your heart from other than us and come to us, for our threshold is lawful to every one who is pure. And patience is the talisman for the treasure of our meeting; whoever unlocks this talisman wins its treasure."

When the sun of tawhīd (the oneness of God) rises, and its rays touch the spirits and its light reaches the insights, the darknesses of the self and the natural temperament are revealed by it, and the spirits move in search of Him to whom nothing is like, and He is the All-Hearing, the All-Seeing. The heart then travels through the wilderness of the command and alights at the stations of servanthood, station after station. It moves from one act of worship to another, while remaining fixed upon one object of worship. The witnesses of the attributes never cease to abide in its heart, awakening it when it sleeps, reminding it when it is heedless, driving it when it travels, and keeping it when it sits. If a witness of lordship and self-subsistence arises in its heart, it sees that the whole affair belongs to God, and that no one has any share of it with Him: ﴿Whatever mercy God opens for people, none can withhold it, and whatever He withholds, none can release after Him. He is the Mighty, the Wise. O people, remember the blessing of God upon you. Is there any creator other than God who provides for you from the heaven and the earth? There is no god but He, so how are you turned away? And if God touches you with harm, none can remove it but He; and if He intends good for you, none can repel His bounty. He bestows it upon whom He wills of His servants, and He is the Forgiving, the Merciful.﴾ ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say: "God." Say: "Have you considered what you call upon besides God? If God intended harm for me, could they remove His harm? Or if He intended mercy for me, could they withhold His mercy?" Say: "God is sufficient for me; in Him the trusting put their trust."﴾ ﴿Say: "To whom belong the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?" They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then remember?" Say: "Who is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the mighty Throne?" They will say: "To God." Say: "Will you not then fear God?" Say: "In whose hand is the dominion of everything, who protects and against whom no protection is given, if you know?" They will say: "To God." Say: "How then are you deluded?"﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 2-89].

If there stands in his heart a witness of divinity, he sees in that witness the command and the prohibition, the prophethoods, the books and the laws, love and good pleasure, dislike and hatred, and reward and punishment. He witnesses the command descending from the One who is established upon His Throne ('arsh), and the deeds of the servants ascending to Him and being presented before Him. He repays the good among them in this abode and, in the Hereafter, with radiance and joy. And He turns to whatever deeds were not according to His command and law, and makes them scattered dust.

If there stands in his heart a witness of mercy, he sees all existence standing in this attribute. The One whose attribute it is has encompassed everything in mercy and knowledge. His mercy extends to where His knowledge extends. So He established Himself upon His Throne by His mercy, so that it might embrace everything, just as His Throne has encompassed everything.

If there stands in his heart a witness of might, greatness, majesty and dominance, then it has another matter.

Thus it is with all the witnesses of the attributes. What we have mentioned is only the slightest indication of them. Unveiling (kashf), direct vision ('iyan) and contemplation (mushahadah) never go beyond the witnesses at all. So let us return to explaining his words.

As for his words, regarding the second degree: "It is the direct viewing of the eye of the heart (mu'ayanat 'ayn al-qalb)." He means by it knowing a thing according to its description, which it has in external reality in every respect. This is impossible with regard to knowing what is in the Hereafter of created things, as Ibn 'Abbas said: "There is nothing in this world of what is in the Hereafter except the names." So how can one know the Lord of the earth and the heavens? The utmost of knowledge is that one's knowledge of Him conforms to His description, either in a general or a detailed manner, detailed in some respects.

His words: "Knowledge that cuts off doubt and is not mixed with bewilderment." This is true. For knowledge, when doubt or bewilderment mixes with it, is not sound knowledge, just as sight of the eye, if it were mixed with such, would not be complete sight. So knowledge is that which cuts off doubt, hesitation and whispering.

His words: "The third direct viewing is the eye of the spirit (ruh), which beholds the Truth with pure beholding."

If by "the Truth" he means the opposite of falsehood, that is, it beholds what is true, in such a way that it is unveiled to it as the visible is unveiled to sight, then it is correct. If by "the Truth" he means the Lord, blessed and exalted, then unless his words are understood as referring to the strength of certainty, increase of faith, and the descent of the spirit into the station of excellence (ihsan), it is false. For the Lord, blessed and exalted, is not beheld in this abode by any eye or spirit. Rather, the knowledge-based likeness is the portion of the spirit and heart, as has preceded.

His words: "The spirits were only purified and honored with permanence, so that they may behold the radiance of the Presence (hadrah), and witness the splendor of might, and draw hearts to the precincts (fina') of the Presence."

He means: the spirits were created for permanence, not for annihilation. This is the truth, and only a small group of people opposed it, from among the people of atheism (ilhad), who say that spirits perish with the perishing of bodies, because they are a power of the bodily powers and an accident of its accidents.

These are two groups. One denies the bodily resurrection (ma'ad al-abdan). The second acknowledges the bodily resurrection and says that God, mighty and majestic, restores the powers of the body and its accidents, and among them the spirit, which perishes with the perishing of bodies. So for both groups there is no spirit subsisting in itself, which dwells with the body and departs from it, connects to it and separates from it.

As for the truth on which the messengers and their followers agreed: these spirits endure after their bodies depart. They do not perish and are not annihilated, and they are blessed or punished in the barzakh (intermediate state). When the Day of Resurrection comes, they are returned to their bodies, and they are blessed or punished along with them. They are not destroyed or annihilated.

So his words: "And the spirits, when they are purified and honored with permanence, to behold the radiance of the Presence," he means the pure and purified spirits. In another copy the reading is "to converse with (lituna'iya) the radiance of the Presence," but the first is more evident and more closely connected to the chapter he titled "the chapter of direct viewing." By "the Presence" is meant the Divine Presence, and by "radiance" (sana') the light that gleams. God, exalted, said: ﴿The flash of His lightning nearly takes away the sight﴾ [al-Nur: 43]. The direct viewing of that is only in the Hereafter, while the one who views here is the light of knowledge and the knowledge-based likeness.

His words: "And witness the splendor of might." Splendor (bahaʾ) in the language means beauty, as al-Jawhari said. From it one says: "bahiya al-rajul" (the man became beautiful), with the vowel kasra, and also "bahuwa," so he is "bahiyy" (beautiful).

Might ('izzah) is used with three meanings: might of strength, might of invulnerability (imtina'), and might of subjugation (qahr). The Lord, blessed and exalted, possesses perfect might in all three considerations. From the first one says "'azza ya'azzu" with fatha in the imperfect; from the second, "'azza ya'izzu" with kasra; and from the third, "'azza ya'uzzu" with damma. They gave the strongest vowels to the strongest meanings, the lightest to the lightest, and the middle to the middle. This might necessarily entails unity (wahdaniyyah), since association diminishes might. It necessarily entails the attributes of perfection, since association contradicts the perfection of might. It necessarily entails the negation of its opposites, and it necessarily entails the negation of any other's likeness to Him in any of these.

So the spirit beholds, by the strength of its knowledge and faith, the splendor of might, its majesty and its greatness. This direct viewing is the result of sound belief that corresponds to the truth in reality, received from the niche of revelation. So no one who stands with the measures of the philosophers, the disputation of the theologians, and the imaginings of the Sufis can hope for it.

His words: "And draw hearts to the precincts of the Presence." The word (fina') is with a kasra on the fa', meaning the side (janib) of the Presence. He means: the spirits, because of the strength of their seeking and the intensity of their longing, drive the hearts and pull them there. For the seeking and movement of the spirit are stronger than the seeking and movement of the heart, just as its direct viewing is more complete than the heart's.

In sum, the rulings of the spirit, according to them, are above the rulings of the heart and more specific than them.

The point is: when the spirit beholds the Truth, it draws all the powers and the heart to its presence, and the heart follows it in submission without resistance. This contrasts with the heart drawing (the body), for the limbs may resist it to some degree and refuse some things with aversion. But as for the spirit's drawing, there is no resistance with it and no refusal.

And success is from God.

The Jihad is of two kinds: jihad by the hand and the spear, and in this, many take part.

The second is jihad by argument and clear explanation. This is the jihad of the elite among the followers of the Messengers, and it is the jihad of the imams. It is the better of the two forms of jihad, because of the greatness of its benefit, the severity of its burden, and the multitude of its opponents. Allah the Exalted said in Surat al-Furqan, which is Meccan: ﴿And had We willed, We would have sent a warner to every town. So do not obey the disbelievers, and strive against them with it, a great striving.﴾

So this is jihad against them by the Qur'an, and it is the greater of the two forms of jihad. It is also the jihad against the hypocrites (munafiqun). For the hypocrites did not fight the Muslims; rather, they were with them outwardly, and perhaps they fought their enemy alongside them. Despite this, Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them.﴾

And it is well known that the jihad against the hypocrites is by argument and by the Qur'an.

This is one of the most refined addresses of the Qur'an and one of its most noble meanings: the believer is always with God against his own self, his desires, his devil, and the enemy of his Lord. This is the meaning of his being of the party of God (hizb Allah), His army, and His allies. He is with God against His enemies, both those who enter into the religion and those who stand outside it. He fights them, opposes them, and angers them for His sake, glorified is He, just as the close companions of a king stand with him in fighting his enemies, while those far from him are idle and unconcerned with that. The disbeliever is with his devil, his self, and his desire against his Lord. The expressions of the early generations (al-salaf) revolve around this.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Dinar, from Saʿid ibn Jubayr, who said: "A helper to the devil against his Lord, through enmity and shirk."

Laith related from Mujahid, who said: "He backs the devil in disobedience to God, helping him in it."

Zayd ibn Aslam said: (ẓahīran) means "supporting" (muwāliyan).

The meaning is that he allies with his enemy in disobeying Him and in associating others with Him, so he becomes, along with his enemy, a helper to him in what incurs his Lord's displeasure.

The special closeness that the believer has with his Lord and his God has now become that of this disbeliever and wicked person with the devil, with his self, his desire, and his companions. For this reason, the verse begins with His words: ﴿And they worship, besides God, that which neither benefits them nor harms them﴾.

This worship is the allegiance, the love, and the contentment with those they worship, which entails their special closeness. Thus they back God's enemies in their enmity toward Him, in opposing Him, and in what incurs His displeasure, unlike His ally, glorified is He, who is with Him against his own self, his devil, and his desire. This meaning is among the treasures of the Qur'an for whoever understands and reflects upon it. And success is from God.

[Section: The difference between tawakkul and ajz (helplessness)]

The difference between tawakkul and ajz is this: tawakkul is an act of the heart and an act of worship, consisting of reliance upon Allah, trust in Him, turning to Him, entrusting oneself to Him, and contentment with whatever He decrees for one, knowing His sufficiency (kifayah), and the goodness of His choice for His servant when the servant entrusts himself to Him, together with his carrying out the means (asbab) commanded and striving to obtain them. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was the greatest of those who relied upon Allah, and he would wear his coat of mail and his armour; indeed, on the day of Uhud he wore two coats of mail, and he hid in a cave for three nights. He was one who relied upon Allah within the means, not upon the means themselves.

As for ajz, it is the suspension of both matters or of one of them. Either a person suspends the means out of helplessness and claims that this is tawakkul, and by the life of Allah, it is indeed helplessness and negligence; or he takes up the means, looking to them and relying upon them, heedless of the Causer (musabbib), turning away from Him, and even if the thought of Him crosses his mind, that thought does not remain with him, and his heart is not attached to Him with complete attachment, such that his heart is with Allah and his body is with the means. Thus his tawakkul is helplessness, and his helplessness is tawakkul.

In this matter, people have divided into two extremes and a middle. (One of the extremes) suspended the means, out of protectiveness toward tawakkul.

The second: suspended tawakkul, out of protectiveness toward the means. (The middle) knows that the reality of tawakkul is not complete except by carrying out the means, so he relies upon Allah within the means themselves. As for the one who suspends the means and claims to be a trusting believer, he is deluded, deceived, and merely wishful, like one who abandons marriage and concubinage and relies upon Allah for children, or abandons plowing and sowing and relies upon Allah for a harvest, or abandons eating and drinking and relies upon Allah for satiety and quenching. The one who relies upon Allah is the counterpart of hope (raja'), and helplessness is the counterpart of wishful longing (muna). The reality of tawakkul is that the servant takes his Lord as his Wakil (trustee), to whom he has entrusted his affairs, just as a principal entrusts his affairs to an agent who knows his sufficiency, his strength, his sincerity, his trustworthiness, his expertise, and the goodness of his choice. The Lord, glorified is He, has commanded His servant to take means, and has undertaken for him that He would bring forth from the earth what suits him; He commanded him to plow, sow, strive, and seek his provision under the guarantee of that, as He has decreed and arranged it and as His wisdom requires. He commanded him not to attach his heart to other than Him, but to make his hope, his fear, his trust, and his reliance rest upon Him. He informed His servant, the Mighty, that He is the One who fulfils the trust and the One who suffices. The helpless one casts all of this behind his back, sits lazily seeking ease, preferring innovation, and says: "Provision seeks its owner as his appointed time seeks him. What has been decreed for me will come to me despite my weakness, and I will not obtain what has not been decreed for me despite my strength. Even if I fled from my provision as I flee from death, it would overtake me." It is said to him: "Yes, all of this is true, and you know that provision is decreed, but how do you know how it has been decreed for you: by your effort or by the effort of another?

If it is by your effort, then by what means and in what manner? And if all of this is hidden from you, from where do you know that it will come to you effortlessly, without striving or toil? How many things have you striven for that were decreed for another, and how many things has another striven for that were decreed as provision for you! When you see this with your own eyes, how do you know that all your provision is by the effort of another?"

Moreover, this objection that I have raised against you, the soul must be made to reject it across all means together with their effects, even regarding the means of entering Paradise and being saved from the Fire. Do you then suspend them relying upon tawakkul, or do you take them up together with tawakkul? Indeed the earth will never be empty of a trusting one who has devoted himself to Allah, filled his heart with trust in Him, hope in Him, and good opinion of Him; yet his heart is constrained from directly engaging in some of the means, so his heart settles upon Allah, finds rest in Him, and trusts in Him.

This (i.e., his trust) was among the strongest means of obtaining his provision. He did not suspend the means; rather, he turned away from one means to a stronger one, so his tawakkul was the most reliable means in his view. His heart's preoccupation with Allah, its tranquility in Him, and its supplication to Him was dearer to him than his preoccupation with a means that would prevent him from that or from its perfection. His heart did not have room for both matters, so he turned away from one toward the other. There is no doubt that this one's state is more perfect than one whose heart is filled with the means and occupied with them away from his Lord. And more perfect than both is one who combines both matters, and this is the state of the Messengers and the Companions. Zakariyya was a carpenter.

Allah commanded Nuh to make the ship, and there was no one among the Companions who suspended the means out of reliance upon tawakkul. Rather, they were the most upright of people in both matters. Do you not see that they exerted their utmost effort in fighting the enemies of the religion with their hands and their tongues, spoke in this regard with the reality of tawakkul, developed and improved their wealth, and prepared for their families their sufficiency of sustenance, following the example of the master of those who rely upon Allah, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and his family.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 25, verse 62:

He mentioned, may He be exalted, the creation of the night and the day and that they are alternating (khilfah).

That is, each of them succeeds the other and does not coincide with it. Had they coincided, the benefit would have been lost through their alternation and their difference.

This is what is meant by the alternation of the night and the day: that each one of them succeeds the other, does not join it, and does not run alongside it. Rather, one of them overtakes its companion and pursues it urgently until it removes it from its dominion; then the other comes after it and pursues it urgently until it defeats it and removes it from its dominion. Thus they are constantly pursuing one another, and neither overtakes its companion.

Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah said: (In exchange and succession (khalaf), one of them stands in the place of its companion, so whoever misses a deed in one of them makes it up in the other.)

Qatadah said: (Perform for God good deeds in this night and day, for they are two mounts that carry people forward to their terms, that bring near everything far off, that wear out everything new, and that bring every promise to the Day of Resurrection.)

Shaqiq said: A man came to ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, and said: "I missed the prayer last night." He said: (Make up what you missed of your night during your day, for Allah, mighty and majestic, made the night and the day a succession (khilfah) for whoever wishes to remember or wishes to be thankful (shukur).)

[Section: On his ﷺ manner of walking alone and with his companions]

When he walked, he would lean forward slightly as he went (takaffu'), and he was the swiftest of people in his gait, the finest of them in it, and the most composed of them. Abu Hurayrah said: "I have never seen anything more beautiful than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it was as if the sun were running in his face. I have never seen anyone quicker in his walk than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it was as if the earth were folded up for him. We would exert ourselves, yet he was not troubled at all."

And 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ walked, he would lean forward as he went, as if he were descending from a slope." On another occasion he said: "When he walked, he would take off (taqalla')."

I say: taqalla' means rising up from the ground entirely, like the state of one descending a slope. This is the gait of those of firm resolve, high aspiration and courage. It is the most balanced of gaits, the most life-giving to the limbs, and the furthest from the gait of frivolity, humiliation and feigned weakness. For the walker either walks in a feigned state of lifelessness, moving as one piece, as if he were a carried plank; this is a blameworthy and ugly gait. Or he walks with agitation and disorder, like a wild camel; this too is a blameworthy gait, indicating lightness of mind in its owner, especially if he frequently turns his head right and left as he walks. Or he walks with gentleness (hawn), which is the gait of the servants of the Most Merciful, as He described them in His Book, saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility﴾.

Several of the early scholars said: with tranquillity and dignity, without arrogance or feigned lifelessness. This was the gait of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. With this gait he would be as if he were descending from a slope, and as if the earth were folded up for him, so that one walking with him would exert himself while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not troubled at all. This indicates two things: that his gait was not a gait of feigned lifelessness or humiliation, but rather the most balanced of gaits.

There are ten kinds of gait. These three are among them. The fourth is sa'y (striding with purpose). The fifth is ramal, which is the swiftest walking with close steps, and it is called khabab. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, the Prophet ﷺ "performed khabab in his circumambulation three times and walked four."

The sixth is nasalan, a light running that does not disturb the walker nor distress him. In some of the Musnads it is reported that the walkers complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about walking during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he said: "Seek help through nasalan."

The seventh is khawzala, which is the gait of swaying. It is said that there is in it a bending and effeminacy.

The eighth is qahqara, which is walking backwards.

The ninth is jamaza, a gait in which the walker leaps in bounds.

The tenth is the gait of tabakhtur, which is the gait of those of vanity and arrogance. It is the gait with which Allah, glorified is He, caused the earth to swallow its owner when he looked at his own sides and was pleased with himself, so he continues sinking into the earth until the Day of Resurrection.

The most balanced of these gaits is the gait of hawn (gentleness) and takaffu'.

As for his walking with his companions: they would walk in front of him while he walked behind them, and he would say: "Leave my back to the angels." For this reason it has come in the hadith that he would drive his companions on ahead. He would walk barefoot and with sandals, and he would walk with his companions individually and in groups. On one of his expeditions he walked, and his finger was wounded and blood flowed from it, and he said:

"Are you but a finger that bleeds,
and in the cause of Allah what you have suffered?"

And when he was on a journey, he would be at the rear of his companions, urging on the weak, carrying them behind him, and praying for them. Abu Dawud related this.

If it is asked: what is the secret in the accusative (nasb) of "salaman" in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Salaman"﴾,
and its nominative (raf') in His words: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant"﴾?
And what is the difference between the two places?

The answer: Allah, glorified is He, praised His servants whom He mentions in these verses with their best attributes and deeds, saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Salaman."﴾
So "salaman" here is an adjunct (sifah) to a deleted verbal noun, which is the saying itself.
