That is: they said a saying, salaman, meaning correct and right, and free from indecency and obscenity, unlike the speech of the ignorant who address them with ignorance. Had "salam" been in the nominative here, the praise mentioned would not be present, but it would imply that when the ignorant addressed them, they greeted them with peace, and this is not the meaning of the verse, nor is there praise in it.
Rather, the praise lies in reporting about them that they do not meet ignorance with its like, but meet it with peaceful speech. This is of the type of "repelling evil with what is better," which none attains except one of great fortune.
The interpretation of the early scholars and their explicit wording is in accordance with this meaning.
Consider how the verse combined their description in the movements of the feet and the tongues with the finest, most refined, most precise and most dignified of them, saying: ﴿those who walk upon the earth with hawn﴾,
i.e., with tranquillity and dignity. Hawn, with a fatha on the ha', is a verbal noun of the thing: "haana, hawnan," meaning it was easy.
From it comes the saying "he walks at his ease (ala hayntihi)." I think it is nothing but a later coinage, yet despite this it is analogically sound, for it is on the pattern of states and conditions, so it is fa'lah from hawn, and its original was hawnah, then its waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it. So the word is sound in its root and morphology.
As for hawn with a damma, it means humiliation (hawan). They gave the strong vowel damma to the strong meaning, which is humiliation, and they gave the easy vowel fatha to the easy meaning, which is hawn. So their walking is described as the walking of forbearance, dignity and tranquillity, not the walking of ignorance, violence and arrogance.
Their speech is described as "salam," so it is the speech of forbearance, tranquillity and dignity, not the speech of ignorance, indecency, obscenity and harshness.
For this reason the verse combines walking and speech. It is not fitting for this noble, great and momentous meaning that its intent be "peace be upon you." So reflect on it.
As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant" (55)﴾,
it is a description of a group of believers among the People of the Book who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Makkah al-Mukarramah and believed in him. The polytheists reproached them and said: "Evil is the delegation your people sent you, to learn the news of this man, and you left your religion, followed him and turned away from your people's religion."
So He reports about them that they addressed them with a speech of disengagement, turning away and gracious abandonment: "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant."
The nominative of "salam" was required, since it is a report of what has occurred. The accusative of "salaman" in the verse of al-Furqan is required, since it is an instruction and guidance toward what is most perfect and preferable for the believer to adopt when the ignorant address him.
So reflect on these secrets; the least of them is worth a journey.
And Allah, alone, is the One praised for what He has bestowed and granted.
Such are the gifts from the Lord of the servants, so nothing is said of "lawla," "hala," or "falma."

(Qa'idah)
Pleasure, as such, is sought by man, and indeed by every living thing. So it is not blamed for being pleasure; it is blamed, and leaving it is better and more beneficial than attaining it, only when it entails the loss of a greater and more perfect pleasure, or when it results in a pain whose occurrence is greater than the pain of its loss.
Here the difference appears between the intelligent, discerning person and the foolish ignorant one, within the bounds of sound intellect. Whenever the difference between the two pleasures and the two pains is elevated, and there is no proportion between one and the other, it becomes easy for him to leave the lesser of two pleasures in order to obtain the greater, and to bear the lighter of two pains to avert the greater.
When this principle is established, the pleasure of the Hereafter is greater and more lasting, and the pleasure of this world is smaller and shorter.
Likewise, the pain of the Hereafter and the pain of this world, and the reliance in that matter is upon faith and certainty. When certainty grows strong and enters the heart, it prefers the higher over the lower in matters of pleasure, and bears the easier pain over the harder. And Allah is the One sought for help.

(Admonition)
Those who worship by night bring near to the camels of the bodies the thread of sleep. When they have taken what fills the need, they raise their heads, and behold, the guide is upon the road, so they set out by the stars that run, one calling the adhan, and another iqamah. The people of resolve are called to prayer in their settlement at night, and the iqamah is given for them at the beginning of the time. Those below them pray at the beginning of the time, and the people of slackness at its end.
When the armies of sleep rush upon the eyes, the watchman of wakefulness cries out to the worshippers: "Prayer is better than sleep." And the sentinel of reproach calls: "He lies who claims my love, until, when the night's darkness covers him, he sleeps away from me." Then the longing one cries out:
"Ask the night about me since your dwellings have gone far,
has it ever closed its eyelids for me in it?"
Then the swift stars pass over the diligent, and they send a message with every path, and its news is conveyed to the caravan of the pre-dawn, and the winds of dawn blow at its arrival, and the one who waits says: "Indeed I smell the scent of Joseph." Glory be to Him who has bestowed existence upon the existing things without their seeking it; then when they found it, they spread out the palms of request seeking its completion. So the fetuses in the wombs of mothers seek the completion of creation; the seed under the soil seeks its sustenance from irrigation; the fruit's marrow awaits from His bounty the completion of its ripening; the ships of the seas are moved by the winds; the merchants await the coming of profits upon them; the students of knowledge ask for the opening of what is closed to understanding; the people of striving seek help over their nature; the wronged one watches for the dawn of victory; the sick one writhes before Him seeking His gentleness; the afflicted awaits the removal of what is upon him; the fearful watches for the messenger of security; the bodies torn apart in the graves await the gathering of the scattered after dispersal; and the brides of Paradise ask for the safety of their husbands and the hastening of the meeting. Then when the creation rises from the layers of the earth at the revival of resurrection, the one who has erred lowers the head of remorse seeking pardon, the worshipper extends the hand of claim against the debtor at the arrival of the term, the ascetic gazes toward the reward of patience, the lover looks down upon the ruins of longing for the beloved, and the knower cries out in the tongue of ecstasy, since no time remains for silence:
"I have a debt with you, how strange,
the debt is mine, and my heart is the pledge."
"Whoever wishes may challenge me in mutual invocation of curse, and let us race at the arrival at the Pool."
Another said:
"I lost my medicine in Iraq, though sometimes
I found in Najd a physician to heal me.
O mountain of al-Rayyan, if you are emptied of them,
I shall clothe you in flowing tears.
Of my roots I do not ask the caravans about them,
and the locks of my longing remain as they were.
Whoever asks the caravans about every absent one
will surely meet a bringer of good news and a bearer of death."

(Another admonition)
The approach of night among lovers is like the shirt of Joseph upon the eyelids of Jacob.
If you love the one served, your heart is present in his service.
"O its dwelling, with grief, for its visit is near,
but beyond that are terrors."
The bride, at the presentation, wears beneath her garments the emblem of fear of rejection, and above her garments the robe of humility, and the redness of shyness suffices her from borrowed rouge, for she does not know to what she will be brought forward. How can one who does not know the outcomes be at ease?
Qays may be placated, but not while the name of Layla is mentioned.
The worshippers are divided into three categories: some looked to the harvest and so increased the seed; some saw the right of the master and so performed it; and some served out of love and longing, and so delighted in the service.
This service has no burden, for its mover is love, while other things are burdensome to the body.
The camels of the bodies of lovers do not feel fatigue, their ears are occupied with the voice of the camel-driver, and their hearts are suspended at the dwelling.
Whoever worships Him out of fear, He grants him safety; whoever worships Him out of hope, He gives him his hope; and whoever worships Him out of love, no soul knows what is hidden for it of coolness of eyes.
"My heart sees her with the eye of longing across the distance,
and so it is favored, but who for my eyes to see her?
Suppose you prevented it from seeing her with its eye,
do you prevent the heart from wishing for her?"
How many a sinner has entered the gathering with a flask of wine in his inner self, and the heat of the sun of remembrance kept working upon it until it turned into vinegar and became lawful.
"It is bitter before you, but when it reaches you,
it meets your fragrance and so becomes sweet."

[Section: The station of humility]

Among the stations of "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" is the station of humility.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63].

That is, with tranquillity and dignity, humble, not wanton, nor exultant, nor arrogant. Al-Hasan said: "They are scholars and forbearing." Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: "They are people of dignity and chastity who do not act foolishly; and if foolishness is directed at them, they show forbearance."

Hawn with a fatha, in the language, means gentleness and softness. Hun with a damma means humiliation.

So the one with fatha is the attribute of the people of faith, and the one with damma is the attribute of the people of disbelief, and their recompense from Allah is the Fire.

And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

Since the humility from them is humility of mercy, compassion, tenderness and submission, He used the particle "ala" (over) for it, implicitly giving these verbs the meanings they carry. For He did not intend by it the humiliation of abasement whose possessor is debased, but rather the humility of gentleness and submission whose possessor is pliant. So the believer is pliant, as in the hadith: "The believer is like a tractable camel." The hypocrite and the wicked are debased. Four types are most profoundly seized by abasement: the liar, the tale-bearer, the miser, and the tyrant.

His words ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ are from might of strength, protection and dominance. 'Ata said: "Toward the believers he is like a father to his son; toward the disbelievers he is like a beast of prey to its quarry." As He said in another verse: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

This is the reverse of the state of those of whom it was said:
"Arrogance toward us and cowardice before your enemy,
the two dispositions are wretched: arrogance and cowardice."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of 'Iyad ibn Himar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has revealed to me that you should be humble, so that none boasts over another, and none oppresses another."

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise."

In the two Sahihs, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I inform you of the people of the Fire? Every harsh, arrogant, proud one."

In the hadith of the argument between Paradise and the Fire: "The Fire said: 'What is the matter with me that only the tyrants and the arrogant enter me?' And Paradise said: 'What is the matter with me that only the weak of people and their outcasts enter me?'"

And it is in the Sahih.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with them both, they said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: Glory is My waist-wrapper, and greatness is My cloak. Whoever contends with Me in either, I will punish him."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, it is related with a marfu' chain (traced back to the Prophet ﷺ) from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', may Allah be pleased with him: "A man will not cease to exalt himself until he is recorded among the tyrants, and then he will suffer what they suffered."

"The Prophet ﷺ would pass by children and greet them with salam."

"A slave woman would take hold of his hand and lead him wherever she wished."

"When he ate, he would lick his three fingers."

"He would be in his house serving his family, and he never took revenge for himself, ever."

He ﷺ "would mend his own sandal, patch his garment, milk the ewe for his household, feed the camel, and eat with the servant. He would sit with the poor, walk with the widow and the orphan to attend to their needs, initiate the greeting with whomever he met, and answer the invitation of whoever invited him, even to the most meagre thing."

"He ﷺ was easy-going in his dealings, gentle in character, noble in disposition, pleasant in company, open-faced and smiling, humble without humiliation, generous without extravagance, tender-hearted and merciful to every Muslim, lowering his wing to the believers, and gentle towards them."

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Shall I not inform you of the one who is forbidden to the Fire, or to whom the Fire is forbidden? It is forbidden to everyone who is near, gentle, soft and easy-going."
Related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: it is a hasan hadith.

He ﷺ also said: "If I were invited to a forelimb or a shank, I would accept, and if a forelimb or a shank were given to me as a gift, I would accept it." Related by al-Bukhari.

He ﷺ "would visit the sick, attend funerals, ride a donkey, and answer the invitation of a slave."

"On the day of Quraizah he rode a donkey, halted with a rope of palm fibre, and had a saddle of palm fibre upon it."

[Section: The sayings of the scholars on humility]

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad was asked about humility, and he said: It is to submit to the truth, to yield to it, and to accept it from whoever speaks it.

It was also said: Humility is that you do not see any worth in yourself. Whoever sees worth in himself has no share of humility.

This is the view of al-Fudayl and others.

Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said: It is the lowering of the wing and the gentleness of the side.

Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: It is that one does not see for himself any station or state, and does not regard anyone in creation as worse than himself.

Ibn 'Ata' said: It is accepting the truth from whoever it comes. Honour lies in humility; whoever seeks it through arrogance is like one who seeks water from fire.

Ibrahim ibn Shaiban said: Nobility lies in humility, honour lies in piety, and freedom lies in contentment.

It is reported from Sufyan al-Thawri, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: The most honoured of creation are five kinds of people: a scholar who is ascetic, a jurist who is a Sufi; a wealthy man who is humble; a poor man who is grateful; and a noble man who follows the Sunnah (the prophetic way).

'Urwah ibn al-Zubair, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: I saw 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, carrying a water-skin on his shoulder. I said: O Commander of the Faithful, this is not becoming for you. He said: When the delegations came to me, listening and obedient, a pride entered my soul, so I wanted to break it.

Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, once held a governorship, and he used to carry a bundle of firewood on his back and say: Make way for the governor.

Zaid ibn Thabit once mounted an animal, and Ibn 'Abbas came forward to take hold of his stirrup. He said: Stop, O cousin of the Messenger of Allah! Ibn 'Abbas said: We have been commanded to do this with our elders. Zaid said: Show me your hand. He brought it out to him, and Zaid kissed it, and said: We have been commanded to do this with the people of the House of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, distributed robes among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and he sent to Mu'adh a costly robe. Mu'adh sold it and with its price bought six slaves and freed them. This reached 'Umar, who then sent him another robe, inferior to the first. Mu'adh reproached him, and 'Umar said: Because you sold the first one. Mu'adh said: What is it to you? Hand over my share. I have sworn that I will strike your head with it. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: My head is before you. And indeed a young man may be gentle with an older man.

Al-Hasan passed by some children who had pieces of bread with them, and they invited him to share. He dismounted and ate with them, then carried them to his home, fed them and clothed them, and said: The hand is theirs, for they have nothing to give except what they fed me, while we have much more than that.

It is mentioned that Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, reproached Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, for his blackness, then regretted it. He threw himself down and swore: I will not raise my head until Bilal places his foot upon my cheek. He did not raise his head until Bilal did so.

Raja' ibn Haywah said: I valued the garments of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was delivering a sermon, at twelve dirhams. They consisted of a qaba' (long robe), a turban, shirts, trousers, a cloak, two leather socks, and a cap.

Muhammad ibn Wasi' saw a son of his walking with an objectionable gait. He said: Do you know how much I paid for your mother? Three hundred dirhams. And your father, may Allah not multiply the likes of him among the Muslims, is me. And you walk with this gait?

Hamdun al-Qassar said: Humility is that you do not see for anyone a need from yourself, neither in religion nor in worldly matters.

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: I have been happy in my Islam only three times. Once I was on a ship with a joking man who said: We were in the lands of the Turks, and the infidel took hold of me like this, and he would take hold of my hair and shake me, because there was no one in that ship more lowly than me. Another time I was ill in a mosque, and the muezzin entered and said: Get out. I could not, so he took hold of my leg and dragged me outside. And another time I was in Syria wearing a fur coat, and I looked into it and could not distinguish between its hair and the lice, because of their great number, and that pleased me.

In another narration: One day I was sitting, and a man came and urinated upon me.

Some have said: I saw in the tawaf a man with guards (shakiriyyah) in front of him, who kept people away from the tawaf on his account. Then after some time I saw him on the Baghdad bridge asking for something. I was astonished at him, and he said to me: I was arrogant in a place where people are humble, so Allah tested me with humiliation in a place where people are exalted.

It reached 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, that a son of his had bought a ring for a thousand dirhams. 'Umar wrote to him: It has reached me that you bought a gem for a thousand dirhams. When my letter reaches you, sell the ring, feed a thousand bellies with its price, and make yourself a ring for two dirhams, and make its stone of Chinese iron, and inscribe upon it: May Allah have mercy on the man who knows his own worth. And Allah knows best.

[The degrees of humility]

[The first degree: humility before the religion]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: humility before the religion. It is that one does not oppose transmitted texts with rational arguments, does not accuse the religion's evidence of being flawed, and does not seek a path to disagreement.

Humility before the religion is submission to what the Messenger ﷺ brought, surrender to him, and acceptance. This is achieved through three things.

The first: that one does not oppose anything he brought with any of the four kinds of opposition that circulate in the world, called: reason, analogy, taste (dhawq), and politics (siyasah).

As for the first: it belongs to the deviant, arrogant people among the theologians, who opposed the texts of revelation with their corrupt rational notions. They said: When reason and transmission conflict, we give precedence to reason and set transmission aside, either by setting it aside through delegation (tafwid) or by setting it aside through interpretation (ta'wil).

The second: it belongs to the arrogant among those who claim to be jurists. They said: When analogy, opinion and texts conflict, we give precedence to analogy over the text and pay no attention to it.

The third: it belongs to the arrogant and deviant among those who claim to be ascetics and Sufis (tasawwuf). When taste and command conflict for them, they give precedence to taste and state, and do not care for the command.

The fourth: it belongs to the arrogant and deviant among the rulers and tyrannical governors. When the Shariah and politics conflict for them, they give precedence to politics and pay no attention to the ruling of the Shariah.

These four are the people of arrogance. And humility is freedom from all of that.

The second: that one does not accuse any of the religion's evidences of being flawed, by thinking that it is of corrupt implication, or of deficient implication, or of limited implication, or that someone else's understanding was better than it. Whenever any such thing occurs to him, let him suspect his own understanding, and let him know that the fault is from him and the affliction is in him, as it has been said:

"How many a critic has found fault with a sound statement, while its flaw lay in a sickly understanding."

Yet minds take from it according to the measure of their capacities and understandings. Likewise, the reality in fact is: no one has accused an evidence of the religion except that the accused one was the one with a corrupt mind, the one whose intellect and mind were defective. So the fault lies in a diseased mind, not in the evidence itself.

And if you see something among the religion's evidences that is difficult for you, and your understanding recoils from it, know that because of its greatness and nobility it has eluded you, and that beneath it is a treasure of knowledge that you have not yet been given the key to. This is with regard to yourself.

As for others: suspect the opinions of men when weighed against the texts of revelation, and let rejecting them be easier for you than rejecting the texts. For as long as you do not do this, you are not upon anything. And if ... and if ... and this is something on which there is no disagreement among the scholars.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah sanctify his spirit, said: The Muslims have agreed that whoever has been made clear the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is not lawful for him to abandon it for the saying of anyone.

The third: that one finds no way at all to oppose the text, neither in his inner heart, nor with his tongue, nor with his action, nor with his state. Rather, if he senses any trace of opposition, it is like the opposition of one who commits adultery, drinks wine, or kills a soul. Indeed this opposition is greater in the sight of Allah than that. It leads to hypocrisy, and it is what the great ones and the imams feared for their own souls.

And know that the one who opposes the text, in favour of the saying of his leader, his shaykh or his imitated authority, or in favour of his own opinion, reason, taste or politics: if he is excused before Allah, and no, by Allah, he is not excused, then the one who opposes his saying in favour of the texts of revelation is more worthy of excuse before Allah, His Messenger, His angels and the believers among His servants.

How strange it is that the falsehood of those who oppose the texts is widely excused on account of having opposed them through taqlid (blind imitation), or through ta'wil, or for other reasons, yet how is the excuse for one who opposes their sayings and the sayings of their shaykhs so narrow, for the sake of agreeing with the texts? How they set snares for him, plotted evils against him, accused him of great offences, and made him worse off than the perpetrators of major crimes! They accused him of their own disease and slipped away from him in confusion, and cast upon him their own misfortune, and made the exaltation of those they follow their refuge and shelter. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

He said: This is not valid except by knowing that salvation lies in insight, that uprightness comes after trust, and that clear proof lies beyond the argument.

He says: What we have mentioned of humility before the religion through these three matters is:

The first: his knowledge that salvation from wretchedness and misguidance lies only in insight. Whoever has no insight is among the people of misguidance in this world and of wretchedness in the Hereafter.

Insight is a light that Allah places in the eye of the heart, by which the servant distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Its relation to the heart is like the relation of the light of the eye to the eye.

This insight is both a gift and an acquisition. Whoever turns his gaze upon the signs and proofs of the truth, and strips himself for Allah of his desires, his insight will be illuminated, and he will be granted a criterion by which he distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

The second: that he knows uprightness comes only after trust. That is, uprightness in speech, action and state cannot be conceived except after trust in the soundness of the knowledge he possesses, and that it is drawn from the niche of prophethood. Whoever is not like this has neither trust nor uprightness.

The third: that he knows clear proof lies beyond the argument. By clear proof is meant the making manifest and apparent of the truth. This comes only after the argument, when it is established: then the truth becomes clear, manifest and evident.

There is another meaning in it, namely: when the servant accepts the proof of God purely through faith, submission and compliance, this acceptance becomes the cause of its becoming clear and manifest, and of its being revealed to his heart. So he is not patient with the clear evidence of his Lord except after accepting His proof.

There is also another meaning in it: that the defect of his deed in its soundness does not become evident to him except after knowledge, which is the proof of God against the servant. So when he knows the proof, what was unclear to him of his knowledge becomes clear through it, and what was faulty of his deeds (becomes clear to him).

There is also another meaning in it: that "wara'" (behind/beyond) is taken in the sense of "amam" (in front of). The meaning is: the proof is only attained by the servant after its clarification. So if it is not clarified for him, there is no proof for him. That is, he is not content with the proof merely by its occurrence without clarification, for clarification is in front of the proof. And God knows best.

[Chapter: The Second Degree is that you are pleased with what the Truth is pleased with for Himself]

Chapter

He said: The second degree is that you be pleased with what the Truth is pleased with for Himself: a servant among the Muslims as a brother, that you not withhold from your enemy a right, and that you accept from the one who apologises his excuses.

He says: If God has been pleased with your Muslim brother as a servant for Himself, will you not be pleased with him as a brother?

So your non-pleasure with him as a brother, when your Master, whom you serve as a slave, has been pleased with him as a servant for Himself, is the very essence of pride. And what ugliness is uglier than a servant's arrogance toward a servant like himself, not being pleased with his brotherhood, while his Master is pleased with his servitude?

From this it follows that the arrogant one is not pleased with the servitude of his Master, since his servitude requires his Master's pleasure with his servant's brotherhood. This is the custom of the slaves of kings: they regard one another as "khushdashiyya" (comrades of the same master) of one another; and whoever among them rises above this is not among the slaves of his master.

His saying: "and that you not withhold from your enemy a right."

That is: the degree of humility is not sound for you until you accept the truth from whom you love and from whom you hate, so you accept it from your enemy as you accept it from your friend. And if you do not withhold his right from him, how would you withhold from him a right that he has against you? Rather, the reality of humility is that when he comes to you, you accept it from him, and when he has a right over you, you discharge it to him. Your enmity toward him shall not prevent you from accepting his right, nor from giving it to him.

As for your accepting the excuses of the one who apologises.

Its meaning: whoever has wronged you, then comes apologising for his wrong, humility requires you to accept his excuse, whether it is true or false, and to leave his inner state to God, Exalted. As the Messenger of God ﷺ did with the hypocrites who stayed behind from him in the expedition: when he returned, they came apologising to him, and he accepted their excuses and left their inner states to God, Exalted.

And the sign of generosity and humility is that when you see a flaw in his excuse, you do not stop him at it nor argue with him, but say: "It may be as you say; and had it been decreed, it would have happened, and what is decreed has no repelling," and the like.

[Chapter: The Third Degree is that you humble yourself to the Truth]

He said: The third degree is that you humble yourself to the Truth, so that you descend from your opinion and your habits in service,

and from seeing your right in companionship, and from your mark in contemplation,

by the word of humility: that you serve the Truth, glorified is He, and worship Him with what He has commanded you, according to the requirement of His command, not according to what you see of your own opinion. Let the motive for you not be the call of habit, as is the motive of one who has no insight, who has merely accustomed himself to a matter and so proceeds upon it. Had he accustomed himself to its opposite, he would have been the same.

Its summary: his motive for servitude is not merely opinion, agreement with desire, love, and habit. Rather the motive is simply the command, while opinion, love, desire and habits are executors and followers, not things obeyed as motives. This is a subtle point that none notices except people of insight.

As for his descending from seeing his right in companionship.

Its meaning: that he should not see for himself a right over God because of his deed. For his companionship with God is through servitude, pure poverty, abasement and brokenness. So whenever he sees for himself a right over Him, the companionship is corrupted, becomes flawed, and hatred is feared from it. This does not contradict what He, glorified is He, has made binding upon Himself of rewarding His worshippers and honouring them. For that is a right which He made binding upon Himself by the sheer generosity, piety, bounty and beneficence of His own. It is not by the merit of the servants, nor that they made it obligatory upon Him by their deeds.

So you must have discernment (furqan) in this place, which is the parting of the ways, and people regarding it are of three groups.

One group saw that the servant is too low and too weak to make a right binding upon his Lord. So they said: nothing whatsoever is incumbent upon God. And they denied the obligation of what He made obligatory upon Himself.

Another group saw that He, glorified is He, made certain things obligatory upon Himself for His servant, so they thought that the servant made them obligatory upon Him by his deeds, and that his deeds were the cause of this obligation. Both groups are in error.

The third group: the People of guidance and correctness said: the servant does not merit from God, by his striving, any salvation or success; no one's deed will ever admit him to Paradise, nor save him from the Fire. And God, Exalted—by His grace and generosity, and the pure bounty of His beneficence—confirmed His beneficence, bounty and kindness by making a right binding upon Himself for His servant by the requirement of promise. For the promise of the Generous is an obligation, even if by "perhaps" and "maybe."

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "'Asa (perhaps) from God is obligatory."

And the promise of the base is a breach, even if accompanied by covenant and oath.

The point: the servant's not seeing a right for himself over God does not contradict what God made obligatory upon Himself and made a right for His servant. The Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may God be pleased with him: "O Mu'adh, do you know what is God's right over the servants?" He said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "His right over them is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. O Mu'adh, do you know what is the servants' right over God if they do that?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Their right over Him is that He not punish them with the Fire."

So the Lord, glorified is He, has no one who has a right over Him, and no striving is lost in His sight, as it has been said:

What right is binding upon Him for the servants? Never; and no striving is lost in His sight.
If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His grace, and He is the Generous, the Vast.

As for his saying: "and descend from your mark in contemplation."

That is: among the parts of humility before the Truth is your annihilation from yourself, for its mark is itself. Descending from it is its annihilation (fana') at the time of witnessing the Presence. This descent may be called acquired (kasbi) in a certain respect, though it is not acquired according to the people of the Path, because it arises at the time of manifestation (tajalli). And manifestation is light, and light overcomes and nullifies darkness, and the mark, according to the people, is darkness. So it recoils from light by its very nature. Thus descent from the mark at the time of manifestation becomes essential.

The way in which it is acquired: it is the result of acquired stations, and the result of what is acquired is acquired. Its fruit, though it arises by necessity in itself, does not preclude that it be called acquired by virtue of its cause. And God knows best.

[Section: On his ﷺ manner of walking alone and with his companions]

When he walked, he would lean forward slightly as he went (takaffu'), and he was the swiftest of people in his gait, the finest of them in it, and the most composed of them. Abu Hurayrah said: "I have never seen anything more beautiful than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it was as if the sun were running in his face. I have never seen anyone quicker in his walk than the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; it was as if the earth were folded up for him. We would exert ourselves, yet he was not troubled at all."

And 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ walked, he would lean forward as he went, as if he were descending from a slope." On another occasion he said: "When he walked, he would take off (taqalla')."

I say: taqalla' means rising up from the ground entirely, like the state of one descending a slope. This is the gait of those of firm resolve, high aspiration and courage. It is the most balanced of gaits, the most life-giving to the limbs, and the furthest from the gait of frivolity, humiliation and feigned weakness. For the walker either walks in a feigned state of lifelessness, moving as one piece, as if he were a carried plank; this is a blameworthy and ugly gait. Or he walks with agitation and disorder, like a wild camel; this too is a blameworthy gait, indicating lightness of mind in its owner, especially if he frequently turns his head right and left as he walks. Or he walks with gentleness (hawn), which is the gait of the servants of the Most Merciful, as He described them in His Book, saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility﴾.

Several of the early scholars said: with tranquillity and dignity, without arrogance or feigned lifelessness. This was the gait of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. With this gait he would be as if he were descending from a slope, and as if the earth were folded up for him, so that one walking with him would exert himself while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was not troubled at all. This indicates two things: that his gait was not a gait of feigned lifelessness or humiliation, but rather the most balanced of gaits.

There are ten kinds of gait. These three are among them. The fourth is sa'y (striding with purpose). The fifth is ramal, which is the swiftest walking with close steps, and it is called khabab. In the Sahih, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, the Prophet ﷺ "performed khabab in his circumambulation three times and walked four."

The sixth is nasalan, a light running that does not disturb the walker nor distress him. In some of the Musnads it is reported that the walkers complained to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about walking during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and he said: "Seek help through nasalan."

The seventh is khawzala, which is the gait of swaying. It is said that there is in it a bending and effeminacy.

The eighth is qahqara, which is walking backwards.

The ninth is jamaza, a gait in which the walker leaps in bounds.

The tenth is the gait of tabakhtur, which is the gait of those of vanity and arrogance. It is the gait with which Allah, glorified is He, caused the earth to swallow its owner when he looked at his own sides and was pleased with himself, so he continues sinking into the earth until the Day of Resurrection.

The most balanced of these gaits is the gait of hawn (gentleness) and takaffu'.

As for his walking with his companions: they would walk in front of him while he walked behind them, and he would say: "Leave my back to the angels." For this reason it has come in the hadith that he would drive his companions on ahead. He would walk barefoot and with sandals, and he would walk with his companions individually and in groups. On one of his expeditions he walked, and his finger was wounded and blood flowed from it, and he said:

"Are you but a finger that bleeds,
and in the cause of Allah what you have suffered?"

And when he was on a journey, he would be at the rear of his companions, urging on the weak, carrying them behind him, and praying for them. Abu Dawud related this.

If it is asked: what is the secret in the accusative (nasb) of "salaman" in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿And when the ignorant address them, they say, "Salaman"﴾,
and its nominative (raf') in His words: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant"﴾?
And what is the difference between the two places?

The answer: Allah, glorified is He, praised His servants whom He mentions in these verses with their best attributes and deeds, saying: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility, and when the ignorant address them, they say, "Salaman."﴾
So "salaman" here is an adjunct (sifah) to a deleted verbal noun, which is the saying itself. That is: they said a saying, salaman, meaning correct and right, and free from indecency and obscenity, unlike the speech of the ignorant who address them with ignorance. Had "salam" been in the nominative here, the praise mentioned would not be present, but it would imply that when the ignorant addressed them, they greeted them with peace, and this is not the meaning of the verse, nor is there praise in it.
Rather, the praise lies in reporting about them that they do not meet ignorance with its like, but meet it with peaceful speech. This is of the type of "repelling evil with what is better," which none attains except one of great fortune.
The interpretation of the early scholars and their explicit wording is in accordance with this meaning.
Consider how the verse combined their description in the movements of the feet and the tongues with the finest, most refined, most precise and most dignified of them, saying: ﴿those who walk upon the earth with hawn﴾,
i.e., with tranquillity and dignity. Hawn, with a fatha on the ha', is a verbal noun of the thing: "haana, hawnan," meaning it was easy.
From it comes the saying "he walks at his ease (ala hayntihi)." I think it is nothing but a later coinage, yet despite this it is analogically sound, for it is on the pattern of states and conditions, so it is fa'lah from hawn, and its original was hawnah, then its waw was changed to ya' because of the kasra before it. So the word is sound in its root and morphology.
As for hawn with a damma, it means humiliation (hawan). They gave the strong vowel damma to the strong meaning, which is humiliation, and they gave the easy vowel fatha to the easy meaning, which is hawn. So their walking is described as the walking of forbearance, dignity and tranquillity, not the walking of ignorance, violence and arrogance.
Their speech is described as "salam," so it is the speech of forbearance, tranquillity and dignity, not the speech of ignorance, indecency, obscenity and harshness.
For this reason the verse combines walking and speech. It is not fitting for this noble, great and momentous meaning that its intent be "peace be upon you." So reflect on it.
As for His words, exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear idle talk, they turn away from it and say, "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant" (55)﴾,
it is a description of a group of believers among the People of the Book who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in Makkah al-Mukarramah and believed in him. The polytheists reproached them and said: "Evil is the delegation your people sent you, to learn the news of this man, and you left your religion, followed him and turned away from your people's religion."
So He reports about them that they addressed them with a speech of disengagement, turning away and gracious abandonment: "To us our deeds and to you your deeds; peace be upon you; we do not seek the ignorant."
The nominative of "salam" was required, since it is a report of what has occurred. The accusative of "salaman" in the verse of al-Furqan is required, since it is an instruction and guidance toward what is most perfect and preferable for the believer to adopt when the ignorant address him.
So reflect on these secrets; the least of them is worth a journey.
And Allah, alone, is the One praised for what He has bestowed and granted.
Such are the gifts from the Lord of the servants, so nothing is said of "lawla," "hala," or "falma."

(Qa'idah)
Pleasure, as such, is sought by man, and indeed by every living thing. So it is not blamed for being pleasure; it is blamed, and leaving it is better and more beneficial than attaining it, only when it entails the loss of a greater and more perfect pleasure, or when it results in a pain whose occurrence is greater than the pain of its loss.
Here the difference appears between the intelligent, discerning person and the foolish ignorant one, within the bounds of sound intellect. Whenever the difference between the two pleasures and the two pains is elevated, and there is no proportion between one and the other, it becomes easy for him to leave the lesser of two pleasures in order to obtain the greater, and to bear the lighter of two pains to avert the greater.
When this principle is established, the pleasure of the Hereafter is greater and more lasting, and the pleasure of this world is smaller and shorter.
Likewise, the pain of the Hereafter and the pain of this world, and the reliance in that matter is upon faith and certainty. When certainty grows strong and enters the heart, it prefers the higher over the lower in matters of pleasure, and bears the easier pain over the harder. And Allah is the One sought for help.

(Admonition)
Those who worship by night bring near to the camels of the bodies the thread of sleep. When they have taken what fills the need, they raise their heads, and behold, the guide is upon the road, so they set out by the stars that run, one calling the adhan, and another iqamah. The people of resolve are called to prayer in their settlement at night, and the iqamah is given for them at the beginning of the time. Those below them pray at the beginning of the time, and the people of slackness at its end.
When the armies of sleep rush upon the eyes, the watchman of wakefulness cries out to the worshippers: "Prayer is better than sleep." And the sentinel of reproach calls: "He lies who claims my love, until, when the night's darkness covers him, he sleeps away from me." Then the longing one cries out:
"Ask the night about me since your dwellings have gone far,
has it ever closed its eyelids for me in it?"
Then the swift stars pass over the diligent, and they send a message with every path, and its news is conveyed to the caravan of the pre-dawn, and the winds of dawn blow at its arrival, and the one who waits says: "Indeed I smell the scent of Joseph." Glory be to Him who has bestowed existence upon the existing things without their seeking it; then when they found it, they spread out the palms of request seeking its completion. So the fetuses in the wombs of mothers seek the completion of creation; the seed under the soil seeks its sustenance from irrigation; the fruit's marrow awaits from His bounty the completion of its ripening; the ships of the seas are moved by the winds; the merchants await the coming of profits upon them; the students of knowledge ask for the opening of what is closed to understanding; the people of striving seek help over their nature; the wronged one watches for the dawn of victory; the sick one writhes before Him seeking His gentleness; the afflicted awaits the removal of what is upon him; the fearful watches for the messenger of security; the bodies torn apart in the graves await the gathering of the scattered after dispersal; and the brides of Paradise ask for the safety of their husbands and the hastening of the meeting. Then when the creation rises from the layers of the earth at the revival of resurrection, the one who has erred lowers the head of remorse seeking pardon, the worshipper extends the hand of claim against the debtor at the arrival of the term, the ascetic gazes toward the reward of patience, the lover looks down upon the ruins of longing for the beloved, and the knower cries out in the tongue of ecstasy, since no time remains for silence:
"I have a debt with you, how strange,
the debt is mine, and my heart is the pledge."
"Whoever wishes may challenge me in mutual invocation of curse, and let us race at the arrival at the Pool."
Another said:
"I lost my medicine in Iraq, though sometimes
I found in Najd a physician to heal me.
O mountain of al-Rayyan, if you are emptied of them,
I shall clothe you in flowing tears.
Of my roots I do not ask the caravans about them,
and the locks of my longing remain as they were.
Whoever asks the caravans about every absent one
will surely meet a bringer of good news and a bearer of death."

(Another admonition)
The approach of night among lovers is like the shirt of Joseph upon the eyelids of Jacob.
If you love the one served, your heart is present in his service.
"O its dwelling, with grief, for its visit is near,
but beyond that are terrors."
The bride, at the presentation, wears beneath her garments the emblem of fear of rejection, and above her garments the robe of humility, and the redness of shyness suffices her from borrowed rouge, for she does not know to what she will be brought forward. How can one who does not know the outcomes be at ease?
Qays may be placated, but not while the name of Layla is mentioned.
The worshippers are divided into three categories: some looked to the harvest and so increased the seed; some saw the right of the master and so performed it; and some served out of love and longing, and so delighted in the service.
This service has no burden, for its mover is love, while other things are burdensome to the body.
The camels of the bodies of lovers do not feel fatigue, their ears are occupied with the voice of the camel-driver, and their hearts are suspended at the dwelling.
Whoever worships Him out of fear, He grants him safety; whoever worships Him out of hope, He gives him his hope; and whoever worships Him out of love, no soul knows what is hidden for it of coolness of eyes.
"My heart sees her with the eye of longing across the distance,
and so it is favored, but who for my eyes to see her?
Suppose you prevented it from seeing her with its eye,
do you prevent the heart from wishing for her?"
How many a sinner has entered the gathering with a flask of wine in his inner self, and the heat of the sun of remembrance kept working upon it until it turned into vinegar and became lawful.
"It is bitter before you, but when it reaches you,
it meets your fragrance and so becomes sweet."

[Section: The station of humility]

Among the stations of "You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help" is the station of humility.

Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the servants of the Most Merciful are those who walk upon the earth with humility﴾ [al-Furqan: 63].

That is, with tranquillity and dignity, humble, not wanton, nor exultant, nor arrogant. Al-Hasan said: "They are scholars and forbearing." Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah said: "They are people of dignity and chastity who do not act foolishly; and if foolishness is directed at them, they show forbearance."

Hawn with a fatha, in the language, means gentleness and softness. Hun with a damma means humiliation.

So the one with fatha is the attribute of the people of faith, and the one with damma is the attribute of the people of disbelief, and their recompense from Allah is the Fire.

And Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, whoever of you turns back from his religion, Allah will bring a people He loves and who love Him, humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

Since the humility from them is humility of mercy, compassion, tenderness and submission, He used the particle "ala" (over) for it, implicitly giving these verbs the meanings they carry. For He did not intend by it the humiliation of abasement whose possessor is debased, but rather the humility of gentleness and submission whose possessor is pliant. So the believer is pliant, as in the hadith: "The believer is like a tractable camel." The hypocrite and the wicked are debased. Four types are most profoundly seized by abasement: the liar, the tale-bearer, the miser, and the tyrant.

His words ﴿mighty against the disbelievers﴾ are from might of strength, protection and dominance. 'Ata said: "Toward the believers he is like a father to his son; toward the disbelievers he is like a beast of prey to its quarry." As He said in another verse: ﴿Severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

This is the reverse of the state of those of whom it was said:
"Arrogance toward us and cowardice before your enemy,
the two dispositions are wretched: arrogance and cowardice."

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of 'Iyad ibn Himar, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah has revealed to me that you should be humble, so that none boasts over another, and none oppresses another."

In Sahih Muslim, from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "No one who has in his heart an atom's weight of arrogance will enter Paradise."

In the two Sahihs, traced to the Prophet ﷺ: "Shall I inform you of the people of the Fire? Every harsh, arrogant, proud one."

In the hadith of the argument between Paradise and the Fire: "The Fire said: 'What is the matter with me that only the tyrants and the arrogant enter me?' And Paradise said: 'What is the matter with me that only the weak of people and their outcasts enter me?'"

And it is in the Sahih.

In Sahih Muslim, on the authority of Abu Sa'id and Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with them both, they said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: Glory is My waist-wrapper, and greatness is My cloak. Whoever contends with Me in either, I will punish him."

In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, it is related with a marfu' chain (traced back to the Prophet ﷺ) from Salamah ibn al-Akwa', may Allah be pleased with him: "A man will not cease to exalt himself until he is recorded among the tyrants, and then he will suffer what they suffered."

"The Prophet ﷺ would pass by children and greet them with salam."

"A slave woman would take hold of his hand and lead him wherever she wished."

"When he ate, he would lick his three fingers."

"He would be in his house serving his family, and he never took revenge for himself, ever."

He ﷺ "would mend his own sandal, patch his garment, milk the ewe for his household, feed the camel, and eat with the servant. He would sit with the poor, walk with the widow and the orphan to attend to their needs, initiate the greeting with whomever he met, and answer the invitation of whoever invited him, even to the most meagre thing."

"He ﷺ was easy-going in his dealings, gentle in character, noble in disposition, pleasant in company, open-faced and smiling, humble without humiliation, generous without extravagance, tender-hearted and merciful to every Muslim, lowering his wing to the believers, and gentle towards them."

The Prophet ﷺ also said: "Shall I not inform you of the one who is forbidden to the Fire, or to whom the Fire is forbidden? It is forbidden to everyone who is near, gentle, soft and easy-going."
Related by al-Tirmidhi, who said: it is a hasan hadith.

He ﷺ also said: "If I were invited to a forelimb or a shank, I would accept, and if a forelimb or a shank were given to me as a gift, I would accept it." Related by al-Bukhari.

He ﷺ "would visit the sick, attend funerals, ride a donkey, and answer the invitation of a slave."

"On the day of Quraizah he rode a donkey, halted with a rope of palm fibre, and had a saddle of palm fibre upon it."

[Section: The sayings of the scholars on humility]

Al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad was asked about humility, and he said: It is to submit to the truth, to yield to it, and to accept it from whoever speaks it.

It was also said: Humility is that you do not see any worth in yourself. Whoever sees worth in himself has no share of humility.

This is the view of al-Fudayl and others.

Al-Junayd ibn Muhammad said: It is the lowering of the wing and the gentleness of the side.

Abu Yazid al-Bistami said: It is that one does not see for himself any station or state, and does not regard anyone in creation as worse than himself.

Ibn 'Ata' said: It is accepting the truth from whoever it comes. Honour lies in humility; whoever seeks it through arrogance is like one who seeks water from fire.

Ibrahim ibn Shaiban said: Nobility lies in humility, honour lies in piety, and freedom lies in contentment.

It is reported from Sufyan al-Thawri, may Allah have mercy on him, that he said: The most honoured of creation are five kinds of people: a scholar who is ascetic, a jurist who is a Sufi; a wealthy man who is humble; a poor man who is grateful; and a noble man who follows the Sunnah (the prophetic way).

'Urwah ibn al-Zubair, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: I saw 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, carrying a water-skin on his shoulder. I said: O Commander of the Faithful, this is not becoming for you. He said: When the delegations came to me, listening and obedient, a pride entered my soul, so I wanted to break it.

Abu Hurairah, may Allah be pleased with him, once held a governorship, and he used to carry a bundle of firewood on his back and say: Make way for the governor.

Zaid ibn Thabit once mounted an animal, and Ibn 'Abbas came forward to take hold of his stirrup. He said: Stop, O cousin of the Messenger of Allah! Ibn 'Abbas said: We have been commanded to do this with our elders. Zaid said: Show me your hand. He brought it out to him, and Zaid kissed it, and said: We have been commanded to do this with the people of the House of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, distributed robes among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, and he sent to Mu'adh a costly robe. Mu'adh sold it and with its price bought six slaves and freed them. This reached 'Umar, who then sent him another robe, inferior to the first. Mu'adh reproached him, and 'Umar said: Because you sold the first one. Mu'adh said: What is it to you? Hand over my share. I have sworn that I will strike your head with it. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: My head is before you. And indeed a young man may be gentle with an older man.

Al-Hasan passed by some children who had pieces of bread with them, and they invited him to share. He dismounted and ate with them, then carried them to his home, fed them and clothed them, and said: The hand is theirs, for they have nothing to give except what they fed me, while we have much more than that.

It is mentioned that Abu Dharr, may Allah be pleased with him, reproached Bilal, may Allah be pleased with him, for his blackness, then regretted it. He threw himself down and swore: I will not raise my head until Bilal places his foot upon my cheek. He did not raise his head until Bilal did so.

Raja' ibn Haywah said: I valued the garments of 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, while he was delivering a sermon, at twelve dirhams. They consisted of a qaba' (long robe), a turban, shirts, trousers, a cloak, two leather socks, and a cap.

Muhammad ibn Wasi' saw a son of his walking with an objectionable gait. He said: Do you know how much I paid for your mother? Three hundred dirhams. And your father, may Allah not multiply the likes of him among the Muslims, is me. And you walk with this gait?

Hamdun al-Qassar said: Humility is that you do not see for anyone a need from yourself, neither in religion nor in worldly matters.

Ibrahim ibn Adham said: I have been happy in my Islam only three times. Once I was on a ship with a joking man who said: We were in the lands of the Turks, and the infidel took hold of me like this, and he would take hold of my hair and shake me, because there was no one in that ship more lowly than me. Another time I was ill in a mosque, and the muezzin entered and said: Get out. I could not, so he took hold of my leg and dragged me outside. And another time I was in Syria wearing a fur coat, and I looked into it and could not distinguish between its hair and the lice, because of their great number, and that pleased me.

In another narration: One day I was sitting, and a man came and urinated upon me.

Some have said: I saw in the tawaf a man with guards (shakiriyyah) in front of him, who kept people away from the tawaf on his account. Then after some time I saw him on the Baghdad bridge asking for something. I was astonished at him, and he said to me: I was arrogant in a place where people are humble, so Allah tested me with humiliation in a place where people are exalted.

It reached 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz, may Allah be pleased with him, that a son of his had bought a ring for a thousand dirhams. 'Umar wrote to him: It has reached me that you bought a gem for a thousand dirhams. When my letter reaches you, sell the ring, feed a thousand bellies with its price, and make yourself a ring for two dirhams, and make its stone of Chinese iron, and inscribe upon it: May Allah have mercy on the man who knows his own worth. And Allah knows best.

[The degrees of humility]

[The first degree: humility before the religion]

He said: It has three degrees. The first degree: humility before the religion. It is that one does not oppose transmitted texts with rational arguments, does not accuse the religion's evidence of being flawed, and does not seek a path to disagreement.

Humility before the religion is submission to what the Messenger ﷺ brought, surrender to him, and acceptance. This is achieved through three things.

The first: that one does not oppose anything he brought with any of the four kinds of opposition that circulate in the world, called: reason, analogy, taste (dhawq), and politics (siyasah).

As for the first: it belongs to the deviant, arrogant people among the theologians, who opposed the texts of revelation with their corrupt rational notions. They said: When reason and transmission conflict, we give precedence to reason and set transmission aside, either by setting it aside through delegation (tafwid) or by setting it aside through interpretation (ta'wil).

The second: it belongs to the arrogant among those who claim to be jurists. They said: When analogy, opinion and texts conflict, we give precedence to analogy over the text and pay no attention to it.

The third: it belongs to the arrogant and deviant among those who claim to be ascetics and Sufis (tasawwuf). When taste and command conflict for them, they give precedence to taste and state, and do not care for the command.

The fourth: it belongs to the arrogant and deviant among the rulers and tyrannical governors. When the Shariah and politics conflict for them, they give precedence to politics and pay no attention to the ruling of the Shariah.

These four are the people of arrogance. And humility is freedom from all of that.

The second: that one does not accuse any of the religion's evidences of being flawed, by thinking that it is of corrupt implication, or of deficient implication, or of limited implication, or that someone else's understanding was better than it. Whenever any such thing occurs to him, let him suspect his own understanding, and let him know that the fault is from him and the affliction is in him, as it has been said:

"How many a critic has found fault with a sound statement, while its flaw lay in a sickly understanding."

Yet minds take from it according to the measure of their capacities and understandings. Likewise, the reality in fact is: no one has accused an evidence of the religion except that the accused one was the one with a corrupt mind, the one whose intellect and mind were defective. So the fault lies in a diseased mind, not in the evidence itself.

And if you see something among the religion's evidences that is difficult for you, and your understanding recoils from it, know that because of its greatness and nobility it has eluded you, and that beneath it is a treasure of knowledge that you have not yet been given the key to. This is with regard to yourself.

As for others: suspect the opinions of men when weighed against the texts of revelation, and let rejecting them be easier for you than rejecting the texts. For as long as you do not do this, you are not upon anything. And if ... and if ... and this is something on which there is no disagreement among the scholars.

Al-Shafi'i, may Allah sanctify his spirit, said: The Muslims have agreed that whoever has been made clear the Sunnah of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, it is not lawful for him to abandon it for the saying of anyone.

The third: that one finds no way at all to oppose the text, neither in his inner heart, nor with his tongue, nor with his action, nor with his state. Rather, if he senses any trace of opposition, it is like the opposition of one who commits adultery, drinks wine, or kills a soul. Indeed this opposition is greater in the sight of Allah than that. It leads to hypocrisy, and it is what the great ones and the imams feared for their own souls.

And know that the one who opposes the text, in favour of the saying of his leader, his shaykh or his imitated authority, or in favour of his own opinion, reason, taste or politics: if he is excused before Allah, and no, by Allah, he is not excused, then the one who opposes his saying in favour of the texts of revelation is more worthy of excuse before Allah, His Messenger, His angels and the believers among His servants.

How strange it is that the falsehood of those who oppose the texts is widely excused on account of having opposed them through taqlid (blind imitation), or through ta'wil, or for other reasons, yet how is the excuse for one who opposes their sayings and the sayings of their shaykhs so narrow, for the sake of agreeing with the texts? How they set snares for him, plotted evils against him, accused him of great offences, and made him worse off than the perpetrators of major crimes! They accused him of their own disease and slipped away from him in confusion, and cast upon him their own misfortune, and made the exaltation of those they follow their refuge and shelter. And Allah knows best.

(Section)

He said: This is not valid except by knowing that salvation lies in insight, that uprightness comes after trust, and that clear proof lies beyond the argument.

He says: What we have mentioned of humility before the religion through these three matters is:

The first: his knowledge that salvation from wretchedness and misguidance lies only in insight. Whoever has no insight is among the people of misguidance in this world and of wretchedness in the Hereafter.

Insight is a light that Allah places in the eye of the heart, by which the servant distinguishes between truth and falsehood. Its relation to the heart is like the relation of the light of the eye to the eye.

This insight is both a gift and an acquisition. Whoever turns his gaze upon the signs and proofs of the truth, and strips himself for Allah of his desires, his insight will be illuminated, and he will be granted a criterion by which he distinguishes between truth and falsehood.

The second: that he knows uprightness comes only after trust. That is, uprightness in speech, action and state cannot be conceived except after trust in the soundness of the knowledge he possesses, and that it is drawn from the niche of prophethood. Whoever is not like this has neither trust nor uprightness.

The third: that he knows clear proof lies beyond the argument. By clear proof is meant the making manifest and apparent of the truth. This comes only after the argument, when it is established: then the truth becomes clear, manifest and evident.

There is another meaning in it, namely: when the servant accepts the proof of God purely through faith, submission and compliance, this acceptance becomes the cause of its becoming clear and manifest, and of its being revealed to his heart. So he is not patient with the clear evidence of his Lord except after accepting His proof.

There is also another meaning in it: that the defect of his deed in its soundness does not become evident to him except after knowledge, which is the proof of God against the servant. So when he knows the proof, what was unclear to him of his knowledge becomes clear through it, and what was faulty of his deeds (becomes clear to him).

There is also another meaning in it: that "wara'" (behind/beyond) is taken in the sense of "amam" (in front of). The meaning is: the proof is only attained by the servant after its clarification. So if it is not clarified for him, there is no proof for him. That is, he is not content with the proof merely by its occurrence without clarification, for clarification is in front of the proof. And God knows best.

[Chapter: The Second Degree is that you are pleased with what the Truth is pleased with for Himself]

Chapter

He said: The second degree is that you be pleased with what the Truth is pleased with for Himself: a servant among the Muslims as a brother, that you not withhold from your enemy a right, and that you accept from the one who apologises his excuses.

He says: If God has been pleased with your Muslim brother as a servant for Himself, will you not be pleased with him as a brother?

So your non-pleasure with him as a brother, when your Master, whom you serve as a slave, has been pleased with him as a servant for Himself, is the very essence of pride. And what ugliness is uglier than a servant's arrogance toward a servant like himself, not being pleased with his brotherhood, while his Master is pleased with his servitude?

From this it follows that the arrogant one is not pleased with the servitude of his Master, since his servitude requires his Master's pleasure with his servant's brotherhood. This is the custom of the slaves of kings: they regard one another as "khushdashiyya" (comrades of the same master) of one another; and whoever among them rises above this is not among the slaves of his master.

His saying: "and that you not withhold from your enemy a right."

That is: the degree of humility is not sound for you until you accept the truth from whom you love and from whom you hate, so you accept it from your enemy as you accept it from your friend. And if you do not withhold his right from him, how would you withhold from him a right that he has against you? Rather, the reality of humility is that when he comes to you, you accept it from him, and when he has a right over you, you discharge it to him. Your enmity toward him shall not prevent you from accepting his right, nor from giving it to him.

As for your accepting the excuses of the one who apologises.

Its meaning: whoever has wronged you, then comes apologising for his wrong, humility requires you to accept his excuse, whether it is true or false, and to leave his inner state to God, Exalted. As the Messenger of God ﷺ did with the hypocrites who stayed behind from him in the expedition: when he returned, they came apologising to him, and he accepted their excuses and left their inner states to God, Exalted.

And the sign of generosity and humility is that when you see a flaw in his excuse, you do not stop him at it nor argue with him, but say: "It may be as you say; and had it been decreed, it would have happened, and what is decreed has no repelling," and the like.

[Chapter: The Third Degree is that you humble yourself to the Truth]

He said: The third degree is that you humble yourself to the Truth, so that you descend from your opinion and your habits in service,

and from seeing your right in companionship, and from your mark in contemplation,

by the word of humility: that you serve the Truth, glorified is He, and worship Him with what He has commanded you, according to the requirement of His command, not according to what you see of your own opinion. Let the motive for you not be the call of habit, as is the motive of one who has no insight, who has merely accustomed himself to a matter and so proceeds upon it. Had he accustomed himself to its opposite, he would have been the same.

Its summary: his motive for servitude is not merely opinion, agreement with desire, love, and habit. Rather the motive is simply the command, while opinion, love, desire and habits are executors and followers, not things obeyed as motives. This is a subtle point that none notices except people of insight.

As for his descending from seeing his right in companionship.

Its meaning: that he should not see for himself a right over God because of his deed. For his companionship with God is through servitude, pure poverty, abasement and brokenness. So whenever he sees for himself a right over Him, the companionship is corrupted, becomes flawed, and hatred is feared from it. This does not contradict what He, glorified is He, has made binding upon Himself of rewarding His worshippers and honouring them. For that is a right which He made binding upon Himself by the sheer generosity, piety, bounty and beneficence of His own. It is not by the merit of the servants, nor that they made it obligatory upon Him by their deeds.

So you must have discernment (furqan) in this place, which is the parting of the ways, and people regarding it are of three groups.

One group saw that the servant is too low and too weak to make a right binding upon his Lord. So they said: nothing whatsoever is incumbent upon God. And they denied the obligation of what He made obligatory upon Himself.

Another group saw that He, glorified is He, made certain things obligatory upon Himself for His servant, so they thought that the servant made them obligatory upon Him by his deeds, and that his deeds were the cause of this obligation. Both groups are in error.

The third group: the People of guidance and correctness said: the servant does not merit from God, by his striving, any salvation or success; no one's deed will ever admit him to Paradise, nor save him from the Fire. And God, Exalted—by His grace and generosity, and the pure bounty of His beneficence—confirmed His beneficence, bounty and kindness by making a right binding upon Himself for His servant by the requirement of promise. For the promise of the Generous is an obligation, even if by "perhaps" and "maybe."

For this reason Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: "'Asa (perhaps) from God is obligatory."

And the promise of the base is a breach, even if accompanied by covenant and oath.

The point: the servant's not seeing a right for himself over God does not contradict what God made obligatory upon Himself and made a right for His servant. The Prophet ﷺ said to Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may God be pleased with him: "O Mu'adh, do you know what is God's right over the servants?" He said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "His right over them is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. O Mu'adh, do you know what is the servants' right over God if they do that?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Their right over Him is that He not punish them with the Fire."

So the Lord, glorified is He, has no one who has a right over Him, and no striving is lost in His sight, as it has been said:

What right is binding upon Him for the servants? Never; and no striving is lost in His sight.
If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His grace, and He is the Generous, the Vast.

As for his saying: "and descend from your mark in contemplation."

That is: among the parts of humility before the Truth is your annihilation from yourself, for its mark is itself. Descending from it is its annihilation (fana') at the time of witnessing the Presence. This descent may be called acquired (kasbi) in a certain respect, though it is not acquired according to the people of the Path, because it arises at the time of manifestation (tajalli). And manifestation is light, and light overcomes and nullifies darkness, and the mark, according to the people, is darkness. So it recoils from light by its very nature. Thus descent from the mark at the time of manifestation becomes essential.

The way in which it is acquired: it is the result of acquired stations, and the result of what is acquired is acquired. Its fruit, though it arises by necessity in itself, does not preclude that it be called acquired by virtue of its cause. And God knows best.

[Section: The Difference Between Moderation (iqtisad) and Deficiency (taqsir)]

The difference between iqtisad (moderation) and taqsir (deficiency) is this: iqtisad is the midpoint between the two extremes of excess (ifrat) and negligence (tafrit). It has two extremes, which are its opposites: deficiency (taqsir) and overstepping (mujawazah). The one who practises moderation has taken the middle course and turned away from both extremes. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who, when they spend, neither are wasteful nor are stingy, but are ever, between that, justly balanced﴾.

And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it completely outstretched﴾.

And He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Eat and drink, but do not be excessive﴾.

The whole of religion lies between these two extremes. Indeed, Islam is a middle course among the religions, and the Sunnah is a middle course among the innovations. The religion of Allah lies between the one who exaggerates in it and the one who neglects it. Likewise, ijtihad is exerting effort in conforming to the command, while extremism (ghuluw) is going beyond it and transgressing it. Allah has not commanded any matter except that Satan has in it two impulses: either toward extremism and overstepping, or toward negligence and deficiency. These are two afflictions, and no one is saved from them in belief, intention and action except the one who walks behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and abandons the sayings and opinions of people in favour of what he brought, not the one who abandons what he brought in favour of their sayings and opinions. These two dangerous diseases have taken control over most of the children of Adam, and for this reason the Salaf warned against them most strongly and frightened those afflicted with either of them about their destruction. Both may combine in a single person, as is the state of most people: he is negligent and deficient in some part of his religion, and extremist and overstepping in another part. The one guided is the one whom Allah guides.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 25, verse 68–70 (part 1 of 3):

It is related in the two Sahihs (al-Bukhari and Muslim) from him (ﷺ) that he was asked: "Which sin is the greatest in the sight of Allah?" He said: "That you set up a rival (nidd) to Allah while He created you." It was said: "Then what?" He said: "That you kill your child for fear that he will eat with you." It was said: "Then what?" He said: "That you commit adultery with the wife of your neighbour." Then Allah the Exalted revealed its confirmation:
﴿And those who do not invoke with Allah another god, and do not kill the soul which Allah has forbidden except in truth, and do not commit adultery﴾ [al-Furqan: 68].

And since the corruption of fornication (zina) is among the greatest of corruptions, and it is contrary to the welfare of the order of the world in preserving lineages, protecting chastity, safeguarding sanctities, and averting what causes the greatest enmity and hatred among people, through each of them corrupting the wife, daughter, sister and mother of the other, and in that is the ruin of the world, it follows the corruption of killing in gravity. For this reason Allah the Glorified joined it with it in His Book, and His Messenger (ﷺ) in his Sunnah, as has preceded.

Imam Ahmad said: "I know of nothing, after killing a soul, greater than fornication."
